subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS

speechtext:
Mr. GLEASON BELZILE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 339, to amend an act respecting the national battlefields at Quebec.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Payment of $100,000 a year for ten years authorized.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext:
This is a most laudable bill. I saw the battlefields many years ago, when the fields and the monuments were in a state of decay. The government has done good work in the past few years in reconditioning these battlefields, and I commend them for what has been done. Canada has not shown the gratitude she owes to her heroes of the past.
I am pleased to see this action to increase the grant to preserve these national monuments, so that they may impress properly the new settlers who come up the St. Lawrence when they first arrive in Canada. As they pass these historic sites they will learn something of the other people who came to Canada in the early days.
I should like to see the principle of the bill applied in the Niagara district. A former Ontario government did good work in reconditioning the battlefields of the war of 1812-14, in which important engagements took place in the Niagara district. There is still, however, a great deal of work to be done there. I hope the government will continue its present policy and make it national in scope. This work of improvement should be a national project, so that we may properly honour the heroes who have served us.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Acquisition of certain lands authorized.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext:
This is an unusual section, inasmuch as it gives notice in advance that

National Battlefields at Quebec
the government, or a government agency, intends to buy a certain tract of land. Normally this would give opportunity to speculators to get in ahead, and then hold up government purchasers for a big price. Have any steps been taken to prevent the government's being held up in this way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: No expenditure is involved in this transaction, other than the normal payment for the necessary deeds and documents. We will acquire this land from the national harbours board, and it will be only a matter of a simple transfer.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Has the parliamentary assistant considered my suggestion of the other evening, namely, to take in some land at the mouth of the Montmorency river, at which point there was severe fighting between Wolfe and Montcalm; also the land on the isle of Orleans where Wolfe's camps were located, and where the lines must be still visible, and at Point Levis, where further lines were established? Is it the intention to include all these historic sites for preservation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: As the hon. member for Davenport knows, most of that part situated east of the city of Quebec, alongside the Montmorency river, is low and marshy. That was the site of Wolfe's first disembarkation. On account of the low and marshy land I do not believe it would be practicable; on the contrary it would be difficult and expensive, to beautify those grounds. I understand that higher up the river and above the falls the fields are now occupied by a golf course and other developments of the kind; the grounds are well cared for, and cairns have been erected to commemorate what happened there. They were put up by the historical society of Quebec.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: What about lie d'Orleans and Point Levis?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: That is farming country, and I do not know what could be done there.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: If the commission are doing any repair work on this property I hope they will not make a mess of it as the national parks commission did at Fort Prince of M ales at Churchill. An old gateway there had fallen down, and they erected a new one of concrete instead of using the old stone with which the other gateway had been built. It spoiled the whole thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that this is a beautiful park that is well kept. This commission endeavours to duplicate what was there before.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Where does federal jurisdiction end and provincial jurisdiction begin in connection with these battlefields?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: The act of 1908 contained a provision under which any province that contributed $100,000 to the fund would be entitled to appoint one commissioner. The provinces of Quebec and Ontario each contributed $100,000 to the fund, and under section 1 of the act they were entitled to appoint one commissioner, while the federal government appointed seven commissioners. The commissioner for Ontario is Hon. William H. Price.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: The government is to be commended for keeping up this memorial and agreeing to pay from the consolidated revenue fund certain sums of money for its development. I understand that the commission consists of seven members.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Seven federal and two provincial; nine in all.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Could not this commission handle other historic sites across Canada, or are their activities confined to this site in Quebec? There are many historic sites across Canada, such as those commemorating the Red River rebellion, which should be kept up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: This commission was appointed to look after the battlefields of Quebec. Other historic sites in Canada are looked after by different boards or commissions.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Is there not an unnecessary expenditure of money when the one commission could handle all the sites across the country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: A fund was raised to commemorate the centenary of the founding of Quebec by Champlain in 1608. Private subscriptions amounted to some $468,000, and the dominion government added $300,000 in 1908, and the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec added another $200,000. There was some money left over from the cost of the celebration, and the commission was set up and acquired the battlefields of Quebec in order to overcome the neglect of the previous years.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Is this commission responsible to the governor in council?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: Oh, yes-to this parliament.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext:
Is the property which it is intended to purchase contiguous to the present site?
National Battlefields at Quebec

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: It is the actual site of the battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759 and of the battle of Ste. Foy in. 1760.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: The new property will be just an extension?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext: The new property is being bought because a road which ran, along the boundary of the park was moved by the municipality of Sillery. This left about 60,000 square feet of land between the old Champlain road-, and the new road. There was a bad curve' there which was straightened out. The commission felt that this land should not be left in the hands of the municipality, because it might be sold to someone who would erect a building and spoil the appearance of the park.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext:
I am not opposed to this bill, but after listening to the discussion it seems to me that this is another example of the national government catering to the provinces which might have $100,000 to enable them to come into this national commission. If the bill were to set up a commission to deal with all of Canada, and money were to be spent for the development of historic sites, I would say it was all right, but I do not like the idea of putting a gun to the head of a province and asking for a contribution of $100,000 so that they may come within the scope of this national commission. It is not a national commission; it i.s a commission to look after historic sites in the two central provinces from a national point of view. That is what it means.
Personally I do not like the idea of perpetuating or glorifying war. I do not like the idea of keeping before our children memories of battles that were fought, of people who died in battle and of victories we were supposed to have won. You do not win anything in a war. As long as we keep reminding our people of war by monuments of this kind; as long as we continue to glorify war and perpetuate the idea of war, we will forget that no one ever wins anything from war. There is nothing to glorify.
I sat on the reconstruction committee in 1942 along with many members of this house. Representations were made by people from every section of the country and every social stratum as to the rehabilitation of this country following war. The consensus of opinion of that committee was that after the second world war was over there were to be no more stone monuments to commemorate it. The whole house endorsed the committee's recommendation that the kind of monument to be erected should be a cultural centre in every section of Canada to commemorate those who

had laid down their lives in the preservation of freedom. I remember hearing representations from the library association, representing all Canada, that a national library should be established, and today in Ottawa a national convention is being held at which that very subject will be discussed. It. disturbs me to find how short are the memories of the members of this house. Everjdjody was agreed then on the kind of monument we should erect, but now, only a few years later, all that seems to have been forgotten. Now we have before us a bill setting up a commission, which is national in name only, since it relates to only two provinces and ignores entirely the principle that was laid down by the reconstruction committee of 1942. These battlefields tend to perpetuate war. The more money you spend on this kind of thing, the more strongly people will feel that there must be other wars. But apparently the government has adopted the policy of catering to a province which can put up $100,000 and is setting up a national commission which will be paid for by the taxpayers of all. Canada; and mind you, every province will contribute its proportionate share, although they are not all included in this scheme. In my own part of the country there are many historic sites, but to have anything done about them you have almost to use a miner's rod to search out who is responsible for earing for them. I wish good luck to Quebec, but the principle of perpetuating war by monuments and that kind of thing is contrary to my way of thinking.
I am disappointed that the recommendations of the reconstruction committee with regard to the development of cultural centres across this country as war memorials are not being carried out by this bill. The bill rather indicates to me that we are going back to where we left off, educating our people in the glorification of war.

subtopic: QUEBEC-PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF $1,000,000 OVER PERIOD OF TEN YEARS
speechtext:
I am afraid that my hon. friend is not familiar with the purpose of the vote before the house. I attended the tercentenary celebration of the founding of Quebec by the great Champlain, and I know that those who were in charge of the program thought that it would be a sad mistake to leave what is now a very beautiful park in Quebec city, which embraces the battlefield of the Plains of Abraham as well as the battlefield of Ste. Foy, to be exploited by anybody and everybody. From the beginning I have been a supporter of this park. As the parliamentary assistant has very well said the purpose of this vote is to acquire additional land to complete the outline of the park, land which might otherwise be acquired by private individuals who would exploit it, so that it would be of no benefit whatever to that great park. It is a

National Battlefields at Quebec
magnificent park, Mr. Chairman, and is very well looked after. There are only two monuments there, one to Wolfe, and the one at Ste. Foy, which suggest that the park was once a battlefield.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South was not fair. He apparently forgot Louisburg, Nova Scotia, where the government took over a very large acreage, restored the old lands, and made a great park out of the territory adjacent to the ruins of old Fort Louisbourg. The same can be said of Fort Beausejour. My hon. friend has been there, I am sure; for he could hardly pass it without going in. All that land around Beausejour has been acquired and made into a beautiful park. People go there to see the museum and admire the park.
I am in accord with that, Mr. Chairman. I do not believe in forgetting the past. I think we should hold more to the past than we have been doing.
Some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia were in order, but he did not seem to know that all our historic sites are looked after by the historic sites and monuments board. No matter where you go in the west you will find monuments erected by the board. They are erecting a number of them now'.

speechtext:
I certainly cannot agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South. Our battlefields in this country show to coming generations what the veterans of the past did to make this country what it is. It would be a shame to allow the Plains of Abraham, Queenston Heights and other battlefields throughout Canada to become overgrown with weeds. Queenston Heights commemorates the days when the French and British fought side by side in the defence of this country. To keep these historic sites in a proper state of preservation certainly will not antagonize the people of the United States, but will remind them of how a handful of people in this country preserved their homes and their freedom. Without such monuments the coming generations would have little to remind them of what the pioneers in Canada did and suffered and died for in order to make this country what it is today.
I do not believe the hon. member for Cape Breton South wants all of these historic sites obliterated. They Should be turned into the finest parks we can possibly make, so that our people will realize that wars do not help us very much. If it is necessary to fight a war for an ideal, whether it is won or lost, the heroes of that war on both sides should be commemorated in a proper manner.

Perhaps I can clear up some of the points that were left in abeyance last evening.
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked some questions with reference to lots 122, 123 and 124, concession 1, west Yonge street. He felt that the sale price in comparison with the purchase price a few years previously was high. I have inquired into the details of the sale and I find that these lots, 122, 123 and 124, concession 1 west of Yonge street, township of East Gwillimbury, are comprised in a parcel of marshland 400 feet wide by 2,400 feet long, 21 acres in extent. This parcel of land was purchased as the site for a proposed channel connecting the east and west branches of the Holland river. The property is low-lying marshland of no value to the department and of little value to anyone else unless reclaimed by diking and pumping. This parcel was advertised, together with other parcels, but no tender being received, the sale price was set by negotiation.
There was a question with regard to weeds, and I assured my hon. friend the member for Muskoka-Ontario that I would look into the matter. I have a statement which I think will meet with his approval. I did not refer the matter to the Department of Justice but to counsel in my own department and the statement, I think, meets the position.
In the first place, there is no statutory obligation to cut weeds growing in navigable

Supply-Transport
waters. Second, the Department of Transport has hitherto cut weeds in the main channels of the Trent canal system, and the department will continue this practice. In the third place, in the case of other channels than main channels of the Trent canal system, where weeds impede the navigation of small boats the department will consider in each case whether it is in the public interest to make an expenditure for cutting weeds. Fourth, the Department of Transport has no responsibility with respect to weed cutting in navigable waters other than in the canals under its jurisdiction.
There was some question last night in connection with the item which provided for the lightship Lurcher, and I was asked why we had not purchased corvettes from War Assets Corporation. There are several technical reasons why corvettes and minesweepers would not answer the purpose. I have them listed here:
The conversion of corvettes and minesweepers was carefully considered by technical officers of the department and they were found to be unsuitable as lighthouse supply and buoy vessels. Here are some of the characteristics which must be present on supply and buoy vessels if they are to function efficiently:
1.	Wall-sided bow in order to approach buoys without causing damage.
2.	Sea kindliness in order to be able to lift buoys in fairly rough weather.
3.	A long well-deck forward and near the waterline in order to facilitate lifting of buoys and providing area for storage of buoys, also anchors and chains.
4.	Considerable cargo capacity.
5.	Shell plates and scantlings in general of rugged construction.
The above requirements are not found in corvettes, which were built for a special purpose; the full form, the general lay-out, their light construction and excessive power make them unsuitable vessels for such alterations.
Corvettes, on account of their size, are not suitable for use as lightships; and minesweepers, in addition to being overpowered, are not of suitable hull shape for use as lightships on exposed stations. The lightship must have much more freeboard than an ordinary vessel and be of a special form so that it can stay on station in all weathers. Furthermore, the ship requires to be fitted with a large amount of special equipment. The main propulsion unit on a lightship vessel is relatively small, thus providing the extra space required for the special equipment. In addition, the lightship requires large bunker and freshwater capacity so as to minimize the necessity of constant attention and the frequent delivery of supply while on station.
Minesweeper hulls, in view of their shape and general lay-out, could not be held at anchor on exposed stations.

Mr. Chairman, I support the principle of this vote for the car ferry and terminals and all the rest of it, of which 81,360,000 is a re vote this year, and I support it because I have always advocated the confederation principle of each for all and all for each. No doubt what is for the good of the maritimes is for the good of the rest of the country. I have always been a believer in that policy, and have never faltered in that belief.
I would point out to the minister, however, that the principle of this vote should be extended to other parts of the country. I could discuss questions in connection with two or three other items but I do not want to take up the time of the committee unduly. We have an old boat, the Northumberland, which came from the same place that is being serviced by this new car ferry. It has been operating in the Niagara district, and when I visited that part of the province last week end I saw people lined up at the station waiting for trains. We need a car ferry to take care of the large volume of traffic that is moving from the Niagara district to Toronto, and there is need also for a car ferry to serve the lake Erie district. Port Dover, Port Huron and Port Stanley are idle because of lack of car ferry service across lake Erie. The provision of an adequate car ferry service in that part of the province would greatly improve the coal situation in western Ontario, and I trust that when the recess comes the minister will seriously get down to that program. The old boat which has been serving the Niagara district for the last thirty years or more was sent up to us because it was not good enough for the maritimes.
The principle of this vote should certainly be extended. In my opinion the time has come for a maritime commission on the great lakes, because what is good for the maritimes or for Ontario or for western Canada is good for the rest of the provinces. I urge the minister to study the situation. I have visited United States ports along these lakes and I can assure the minister that we are miles behind them in marine services on the upper great lakes.

I wish to make a few remarks about transportation problems at
Supply-Transport

Borden and Tormentine. In the first place, I wish to compliment the minister and his department on the excellent motor vessel Q.S.M.V. Abegweit. It is without doubt the best icebreaker in the world. Last winter, although the ice was not abnormally heavy, it was the usual kind of season and the ferry was able to keep to its schedules with reasonable regularity. This is commendable, and I am sure our winter transportation problems are solved. But we still have a bottleneck at Borden and Tormentine. I submit that as long as we have a ferry operating on two services-by that I mean operating for railway and operating for automobile and bus traffic-we shall continue to have difficulties. If the trains are late, the ferry must wait to take over freight cars, express cars, mail cars and passengers. Consequently long lines of automobiles are delayed in the heat at Borden or Tormentine and often must wait one or two hours before crossing.
1 believe this bottleneck would be lessened if we had an auxiliary ferry. An auxiliary ferry would not cost very much, because it would not operate in the wintertime and would not need to be built as strongly as the present Abegweit. If we had such an auxiliary steamer it could operate on schedule and tourists or other persons wishing to cross over in automobiles or trucks would know with reasonable certainty when the crossing could be expected and would not be there waiting many hours in the heat for a crossing. This would materially help our tourist industry and would also help the export of products of the farm and sea.
I was pleased that the minister was able to have the railway car deck planked to permit trucks to drive off and on under their own power. During the past autumn and this spring trucks loaded with perishable products often had to wait from one to two hours for a crossing. If you had a load of smelts or lobsters going to New York, Boston or Philadelphia, this loss of time was important and often discouraged the shipping of such products to those markets.
I urge upon the minister the necessity of exploring the possibilities of procuring an auxiliary steamship solely for the purpose of carrying automobiles and trucks. I am sure that if such a steamer is available, and if the docks can be made to accommodate it, our transport problems will be much lessened in the future. I would ask the minister to give this matter his best consideration.

I commend the minister for the work that is being done in constructing the car ferries and building the terminals serving Prince Edward Island. The people in that province have waited many long years for this. It is pleasing to know that the new ferry steamers operated so satisfactorily during the winter.
Before this item of $3,547,000 passes I should like to have some further information from the minister. How much of the vote is payable on account of the new car ferry? What is the total cost of the car ferry up to the present time? I should also like to know how much of the appropriation is for construction of the terminals on the Cape Tormentine and Borden sides, and what the total expenditures are for the building of these terminals. Will the minister also indicate whether this appropriation will satisfactorily complete the terminals at both landing points?

The total estimated cost of the terminals at Tormentine and Borden wras $6,622,000. That estimate was made about a year ago, and had to be revised again this year because of certain increases. It is now fixed at $6,877,900. The hon. gentleman knows of course that all this work is under the supervision of the Canadian National Railways. They are acting as agents for the government. Thus far $3,330,000, including $98,000, has been spent. That money was spent last year and a portion, $3,547,000, is to be spent this year. Of the amount of the estimates, $1,360,000 is a revote. The Canadian Dredge and Dock have the contract for the work at Tormentine, and it is about sixty-four per cent complete.
Is that a lump sum contract, or a cost plus contract?

Oh, it is not cost plus. I would think there is an escalator clause in the contract. I understand the Canadian National Railways have proceeded in that manner. I must say however that in connection with one of these points-I am not sure whether it was Tormentine or Borden-we were not able to get a contractor to do the work. There were no answers to our advertisements, so we had to proceed by way of negotiation.
At Borden the contractor is Foundation Maritime Limited. They have completed a little more than fifty per cent of their work.
Supply-Transport

It is expected that the Tormentine terminal should be completed by about the middle of May or June, 1949, and it is expected that the work at Borden will be completed at about the same time.
At what place was the department unable to secure a contractor?

I am speaking from memory, and for that reason I do not wish to be held too closely to what I say. I believe, however, it was for the work at Borden. The department advertised but received no bids. This was a time when material costs were high.
I understood from the minister that the work was proceeding at Borden.
Oh, yes; we finally gave a contract. But we had difficulty in getting a contractor to do the work.
What was the name of the contractor?

At Borden the contractors are Foundation Maritime Limited and Canadian Dredge and Dock Company. The Canadian Dredge and Dock Company have the contract for the work outside the jetty, including the extension and filling, and inside the jetty the construction is being done by Foundation Maritime Limited.
The hon. member asked as to the final cost of the Prince Edward Island car ferry. Again I speak from memory, but I believe it is a little over $7 million. I would not like to say whether it is $7,200,000 or $7,100,000.

Will the
appropriation now before the committee complete the terminals at Tormentine and Borden?
I am informed it will. This year we are going to spend $3,500,000, and we have already spent $3,300,000. That makes the revised estimate of $6,800,000 which I gave a few moments ago.

Would the minister mind putting a little information on the record? In answer to the hon. member for Cumberland the minister said that the contract under discussion was cost-plus, but that it contained an escalator clause. What is a contract with an escalator clause? What i3 the difference between the two?

A cost-plus contract, as I understood it during the war years, is a contract which provides the payment of a certain fee for the work done, plus cost. To

the contract are annexed memoranda of the items of cost which may be charged. There may be twenty-five or there may be ten items of cost. The escalator clause does not include a series of cost items, but it does provide that if there is an increase, for instance, in wages and materials after the contract has been entered into, such increase may be charged up in addition to the fixed amount of the contract, always subject to audit.
In effect there is not much difference.
Oh, yes.

If that is so, why does the Department of Public Works hold up a job every year-and I think it is still being held up-for a dry dock at Saint John, New Brunswick, because they did not want a contract with an escalator clause? Is the escalator regulated to work both ways, or does it just go up? Is it regulated so that it will work the other way? My understanding is that a contract is based upon an estimate; ' then if you are out one way or another in your figures, or if there is additional cost, such as wages or the like, the escalator clause provides that you can revise the figure. But where a contract is let in which a large amount of money is involved, does the escalator clause permit departmental officials to turn the machine downward so as to protect public funds if it develops that the estimate was too high?

The contract in which there is an escalator clause proceeds on the assumption of a basic amount. If wages rise above that, the escalator clause provides for an increase. There is no provision for decrease.
It is not only a matter of wages, though?

I was out of the chamber for a few moments and I did not hear anything that was said under this vote. I wish to say a few words about the ferry system between Borden and Tormentine.
As an outsider I know that there was great difficulty in getting people to tender for the contract work on the Borden side, but the work that has been going on for the past six months under a cost-plus contract is proceeding most satisfactorily. Some hon. members may feel that the vote from time to time for the Borden-Tormentine ferry involves a large amount of money. In actual fact it is only a small amount for the service which the island province requires. Prince Edward Island is the only island province in the

Supply-Transport
dominion, and to the people down there transportation is vital. Over sixty-five per cent of them make their living from agricultural pursuits. During the war our province made a real record in production of the sinews of war, and the farmers are still producing.
For the benefit of some hon. members who may feel that the expenses of our transportation system are high, I should like to place some figures on the record. Let me point out at the beginning that these expenditures are due us under the contract made with us in 1873. The freight handled on the Borden-Tormentine ferry is one of the best-paying freighbhandling operations of the Canadian National Railways system.
I prepared these figures a few days ago, and I had to take those for the month of April. Outward freight figures for that month show that 1,415 cars of potatoes w'ere ferried in April, 1948, from Prince Edward Island to the mainland, or almost 500 cars more than in 1947. The total cars ferried to the end of April for the crop season was 7,046. Practically all of these were for long-haul shipments-the most beneficial from the point of view of the railways. But that was not the only freight ferried in April. In addition there were 20 carloads of eggs, 75 carloads of livestock, 20 carloads of meat, 15 carloads of pulpwood- and ninety per cent of all this was for long-haul carload shipments. Besides these larger movements there were many smaller ones.
I have been referring to the outward freight, but the inward freight is also long-haul freight. There were 119 cars of coal; 40 cars of hay; 24 cars of automobiles; 175 carloads of fertilizer; 245 carloads of flour and feed; 40 carloads of cement; 14 carloads of fruit; 18 carloads of soft drinks-because, as you know, ours is a prohibition province; 15 carloads of sugar and 6 carloads of molasses. In both inward and outward freight there were over 2,500 cars during the month.
When someone gets up and says that this is a large amount to pay for a steamer, I say: No ; we should really have another steamer to assist in carrying our freight. I am not going to urge that at the present time, but I do want to say to the committee that the outgoing and incoming freight that has been produced is simply wonderful for Prince Edward Island. Nothing is too good for our farmers in the way of transportation, and that is why from time to time we advocate better truck service. At the present time the truck service is not what it should be for the exporting of farm products.
The minister said the other day that they were going to plank at least part of the deck 5849-318
of the Abegweit, either with wood or with steel, so that trucks could run on under their own power. I submit that there should be no freight charge over and above what it costs to haul the same freight by truck over a highway. This question has been debated at many sessions, and we did succeed in having truck charges reduced by about fifty per cent. But they should be reduced so that the terms of union in 1873 will be met, and one of those terms was that the ferry should be treated simply as a highway.
Can the minister give the committee definite assurance that the Abegweit will be ready for service before July 1?
The information I have is that the planking will take about fourteen days and that the vessel should be in operation in plenty of time to look after the tourist traffic.

As one who has advocated an improvement in the service between the mainland and the island, I want to express my appreciation of the minister's efforts in this connection. He visited the area and made his own investigation, as others have done, and it is pleasant to observe his interest. When I was there last summer I examined, as I had done before, both terminals, and I would like to know whether they would consider a boat that might be specially designed for truck and automobile service. I am thinking of a ship something like the large ones on the great lakes which ferry only trucks and motorcars. The tourist traffic to the island is increasing greatly, as it should, but it will be retarded unless the tourist can get on and off the island more rapidly than he can today.
The facilities at the Wood Island end are not exactly what they should be, and I am sure that if the minister goes there he will decide to improve them. At the Borden end it should be possible to have cars get on and off the boat more quickly. The present ferry is good, but too large to permit this kind of entry and exit. I strongly urge upon the minister that he consider building a boat specially designed for motorcars and trucks which could run in between the trips of the larger boat. WThen I examined the docks I could not make up my mind that they would be suitable for a low-level motorcar and truck traffic ship.

501. Strait of Canso

Transportation improvements and facilities-capital (revote $260,000), $500,0-00.

I read in the newspapers a report that new ferries were to be provided. I am not particularly opposing that, but I think
Supply-Transport

ferries are outmoded for this particular area. The minister has shown a good deal of vision, and I should like him to consider eliminating the question of a ferry. There is no place for car ferries in these modern times, especially across a strait of that'width. They were all right years ago, but in these days they are too slow. They retard traffic and increase costs beyond what they should be.
This is an ideal location for a bridge. I have surveyed many large bridges, but perhaps I could mention some that I have not surveyed. I am going to try to get down to see the gigantic bridge at Sydney, Australia, which spans the great harbour entrance there. There is no reason why there could not be a similar bridge across the strait of Canso. The minister frequently goes to New York, and he must have seen the gigantic bridge across Hell Gate. There are two giant bridges at San Francisco which span a much greater distance than would have to be spanned across the strait of Canso. At St. Louis there are great bridges across the Mississippi, and they are planning the construction of six more. They are also planning the building of two more very large bridges at San Francisco.
A bridge increases traffic; a ferry retards traffic. Of course if there is no ferry or bridge, there is no traffic. In this day and generation a ferry in that area is altogether outmoded. I strongly recommend to the minister that he keep before him the desirability of bridging that strait. It would not have to be an exceptionally long bridge; I doubt if it would be as long as the bridge at Quebec. It certainly would speed up traffic considerably between Sydney and Montreal and Toronto, and would pay for itself by the reduction in freight charges that would accrue over the years. It would make for expansion of all business in that part of Nova Scotia. I am not opposed to the vote, but I am opposed to the continued use of ferries in preference to bridges.

I am not going to make a speech on this subject; I think I have made enough of them. A bridge across the strait of Canso is one of the main issues in the province of Nova Scotia today. In these estimates there is an appropriation of $250,000 to improve the existing ferry facilities. To those who think the government really means something in continuing to survey the possibilities of a bridge across that strait, it looks strange to see such a large amount spent on improving the present facilities.
I questioned the minister in the house a short time ago as to the progress that is being made by the commission of engineers appointed by his department, and when he expects to

receive their report. His reply was, the latter part of July. That was recorded in the press, and I have received several letters about it since. Throughout the province of Nova Scotia organizations have been formed-nonpolitical organizations, religious societies, veterans' bodies, and the like-which meet all over the province weekly. Their purpose is to press upon the government the necessity of improving the transportation facilities between the mainland and Cape Breton island, which would also do much to relieve the unemployment problem. The people down there appreciate the fact-and I think it is not generally appreciated throughout Canada- that one-third of Canada's basic steel, and perhaps half of all the coal produced in Canada, is produced on the island of Cape Breton. Yet these products have to be dragged out from Cape Breton island by the present outmoded transportation facilities. I know the minister realizes that, but apparently he is tangled up with incompetent engineers or with the treasury branch.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps both.

Maybe both. I am continually receiving letters and resolutions asking what the government is going to do about this bridge across the strait of Canso. I do not bother the minister any more with them, because I feel sorry for him. I feel that he would have built it long ago, if left to himself, if only to stop me and the hon. member for Davenport from talking. The letters I get are to this effect: What is the government doing about it? Is it trying to fool us? They have been making borings for a long time, and they know how deep the water is; they have had several engineers' reports. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I received a return on this subject that would fill this desk; yet in spite of all the information the government has, it appointed an engineering commission to make further investigations. The letters I receive go on to ask: Why is the government continuing to spend half a million dollars on improving present facilities if it is really in earnest about building this bridge? They feel that the government does not intend to build it, or that something is wrong somewhere.
Another point they make is this: It is strange that the minister expects to get a report from his engineers only after the house closes. Why could not this engineering commission make a report now, with the information already available, information which has been gathered over the years? I personally think that the engineers could have come to a conclusion before the end of July. Anyway I have promised myself that towards the end of

Supply-Transport
July I shall come to Ottawa and I would like to meet the minister at that time and those who are going to finalize the engineering report; I am sufficiently interested in the matter to do that. I suggest to the minister that if he hustles up that report it will relieve the minds of the people of Nova Scotia; for they are beginning to mistrust the intentions of the government in spending money on the survey of a project which apparently they have no intention of going ahead with, because at the same time they are spending a large amount of money to improve the existing transportation facilities.
We were discussing here this morning an item of $3,500,000 for a car ferry for Prince Edward Island. Anyone who has travelled in the United States knows that if the Americans were in this country they would have had a tunnel between those islands long ago. It is in our own interest to do that. But it is a dead horse in this house so far as I am concerned. While I have a great deal of confidence in the minister himself, I am beginning to look behind the scenes. I think he is being pulled hither and yon. I would ask him before this house closes to make some statement on the building of a bridge across the strait of Canso, so that I can go home and reassure the people of Nova Scotia that everybody is not dealing dishonestly with them but that there is some evidence of going ahead with this very necessary national improvement. And it is a national improvement, because it would affect not only Cape Breton but everything clean through from Cape Breton to Moncton. The transportation facilities on the C N.R. are good from Montreal to Moncton, but not so good from Moncton to Sydney. They need overhauling. I trust that the minister will make a statement before the house closes that will be sufficiently definite for me to be able to say something definite to the people back home.
I think I can-

Before the minister replies, Mr. Chairman, I wish to add my voice in support of the representations made by the last two hon. members in regard to the Canso strait project. I do not propose to speak at any length, because the minister is going to reply and he is quite familiar with the subject which has been placed before the committee by the hon member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Davenport on more than one occasion, as well as by other hon. members from the maritimes.
I would ask the minister whether he is familiar with the brief presented by the transportation commission of the maritime board
5849-318i
of trade with regard to the proposed bridge or causeway, and if so, to deal with the various points outlined in that brief. I would also ask him whether he has ever read the representations made before the rehabilitation committee of this house about three or four years ago by the then premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. A. S. MacMillan. The brief goes into the matter fully and deals with the report prepared and presented by Mr. D. W. McLachlan, of the Canadian National Railways, whom we all recognize as an authority and a man of vast experience. I would ask the minister to deal with the figures presented by Mr. McLachlan, and not to stop at the boring surveys which are now under way.
I do not always agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I did not agree with him yesterday, when I think he was entirely out of his field; but today he is dealing with something of which he has an intimate knowledge, and something which is directly connected with that part of the country. We are all interested in the development of Cape Breton and the mainland, as well as the rest of Canada. We want to see steps taken which will bring about a greater opportunity in Cape Breton for the development of the coal and steel industries. It is a well known fact that the shipment of coal is handicapped because of the lack of proper facilities. That has all been set out. The realignment of the Canadian National Railway tracks to provide necessary and suitable "haulage is all set out in the report to which I refer. The costs are given, the distance and the type of bridge are mentioned. The whole thing should be carefully studied and a statement made by the minister. Perhaps he is not in a position to do it today, but it should be done at some time.
The report refers to the amount of coal which was shipped in the various years, particularly in 1937 and thereafter. It is with that thought in mind, the shipment of greater quantities of coal to the mainland and in turn to central Canada to increase the prosperity of the coal fields of Cape Breton, that I join with other hon. members in urging the minister to give greater consideration to this matter and to tell us what he is willing or anxious to do to help the economy of that section of our country.

I wish to add my voice to what has been said by the hon. member for Davenport, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the senior member for Halifax. There is one undertaking on which the 650,000 people of Nova Scotia speak with
Supply-Transport

one voice, namely the construction of this bridge. There is a feeling throughout Nova Scotia, and I have it too, that there has been unnecessary procrastination on the part of those in authority at Ottawa. The senior member for Halifax has just said that Mr. A. S. MacMillan, who was the premier of Nova Scotia at the time, returned from Ottawa before the last election and announced that he had had a commitment from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply that the bridge would be built. Why it takes so long to get the information, as pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I do not know. Surveys have been going on for many years. Surveys have been made within the last two years. Engineers have been appointed to review the plans. Why they cannot accept the figures and bring down their report, even if it is only a progress report, and let us know what their views are, I do not know. I should like to know why it is put off continually and why there is so much procrastination. The people of Nova Scotia do not understand it.
I was minister of highways in Nova Scotia for over eight years. When I first became minister there was inadequate ferry service for highway traffic. We had wharves and ferry boats built. The service was improved; but it appeared to me every time I went to Cape' Breton that it was a logical and necessary undertaking to have a bridge or causeway over the strait of Canso. The distance is short, and the foundations are good. I do not understand why there is so much delay. Anyway, I want to repeat that the people of Nova Scotia demand this and require it. In that respect they speak with one voice. I am glad to join with other hon. members who have expressed their views today.

I think I can make as accurate a statement on Canso now as I could even if I acquiesced in the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South that further information be obtained before the house rises. The position is simply this. In July of last year I made a statement in the house outlining the position at that time. I explained the various projects under consideration: a causeway, a bridge, improved facilities and the realignment of the line. I went into it at great length. As I then said, it was a report which was prepared by the engineer, who had already given careful consideration to the brief of the maritime board of trade, to which the senior member for Halifax referred, as well as the presentation made by the former premier of Nova Scotia. Following the decision reached by the officers of the department, an item was

placed in the estimates. However, following that, the premier of Nova Scotia and a delegation from that province waited upon the then minister of reconstruction and supply and myself. This matter was fully discussed. I am not free to state here what was said at that time, but there was an engineer with the group that came up, the premier himself, and one other individual. Certain aspects of the scheme were put forward, and we promised to give it further consideration.
Later the proposal was made that we set up a board of engineers to review the reports and special surveys previously made by the Department of Transport. That committee has been appointed. It consists of three engineers, Professor D. S. Ellis, Dr. A. Surveyer and Dr. P. L. Pratley. These men have gone to the scene, have consulted with our officers and are studying whether or not it is practicable from the several standpoints to construct a bridge capable of accommodating a singletrack railway and highway traffic, to construct a causeway for a railway and highway traffic, to construct a tunnel for highway and railway traffic, and the provision of improved railway facilities and ferry service. That board was appointed only in January of this year. The factthat it will not report until July has no significance. I can assure my hon. friend that if he comes up here after they have reported I shall certainly be delighted to see him, as I am at any time.
There seems to be some apprehension about the amount of money that was spent last year. While $250,000 was voted, only $20,000 has been spent. That amount was expended because the borings were not completed and it was not possible to spend a greater sum. As mentioned in the statement made last year, a decision was reached to improve the facilities, and that would cost $4,500,000. This amount is placed in the estimates in order to provide for the beginning of the work. The facilities are not good. They will have to be improved in any event, pending the finding of the board, and if it is decided that a scheme other than this should be proceeded with, the money simply will not be spent. So that until such time as the board of engineers has reported, I am afraid I am not able to add anything to what I have already said.

I should like to bring one other point to the minister's attention. Taking into consideration the $5 million estimated as the cost of the ferry, and the twenty per cent saving which Mr. Fairweather estimated would be made by the realignment of the tracks-

Supply-Transport
The cost of the ferry is about 81,500,000, not $5 million.

Taking the cost of the ferry at $1,500,000, and against that the saving which would be effected if the tracks were realigned, what is the minister's long-range view as to the saving that would be made by the Canadian National Railways? It is shown in Mr. Fairweather's report that whereas the largest type of locomotives from Truro to Moncton can take a haul of 1,930 tons, from Moncton to Edmundston they are capable of hauling 3,500 tons; or, to state it in the equivalent of cars, from Sydney to Port Tupper, 21 cars; from Mulgrave to Stellarton, 17; from Truro, Nova Scotia, to Moncton, 26; and from Moncton to Edmundston, 45. They are able to haul about twice as many cars from Moncton to Edmundston as they can over the line of track the realignment of which is being considered. The fact that the realignment was not done, no doubt added to the C.N.R. deficit of last year. And when you remember that 78-2 per cent of the revenue came from freight, I suggest that it is an important item and we should consider whether it is feasible and good business to carry out the project that is suggested.
It is roughly estimated by Mr. Fairweather, in his evidence before a parliamentary committee, that an improved railway from Sydney to Moncton would result in a twenty per cent reduction in the cost of moving freight over that line, and that twenty per cent would naturally be reflected in the price of coal and steel shipped to central Canada.
I am informed that the saving in railway operations would be $300,000.
For what period?
Per annum.
And against that you pay the interest tied up in the $1,500,000, operation costs, and so on. Can we get a picture of the whole thing so that we may see it from the sound business point of view?

Are special efforts being made under the minister's direction to improve the grades and alignment of the road from Moncton to Sydney? Are steps being taken in this direction by the Canadian National? Can the minister say what is practicable in the circumstances, what the cost will be, and how soon the work will be undertaken?

The engineer in the department went into the question fully. The hon. member no doubt remembers that evidence was given in the committee before I
made the statement referred to a moment ago, and the Canadian National Railways have come to the conclusion that the capital cost would be such that they could not approve
its being done.

If the proposal cannot be carried out in its entirety so as to bring the whole road up to the highest state of perfection, can the minister say whether those sections where the greatest difficulty is encountered now could be improved and brought up to a satisfactory standard?

One word in reference to the strait of Canso. The hon. member for Cumberland said that Nova Scotia would speak with one voice on anything that made for improved conditions at the strait of Canso, and I add that Prince Edward Island would be happy indeed to see the construction of either a bridge or a causeway, or whatever the engineers decide should be undertaken, to take care of traffic at that point. We produce foodstuffs for which we could find a home market in Sydney. According to statistics-the hon. member for Cape Breton South will correct me if I am wrong-over $50,000,000 a year is paid out in wages there alone, and that is not the only amount that is distributed in wages. If a bridge or causeway were erected, farmers in Prince Edward Island would benefit because they could take their trucks direct into Sydney, where they would find an excellent market. I can assure the hon. member for Cape Breton South that Prince Edward Island would take the same view as that expressed by the hon. member for Cumberland, We are prepared to support anything that may be undertaken for the benefit of the three maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The rest of us, too.
So what is holding it up?

One more question. I have never been able to get figures in connection with freight originating in the maritimes and going to central Canada, or from the Atlantic to the central region. How.does the minister arrive at the $300,000 that was mentioned a moment ago?
I cannot give the answer; I do not know.
You have experts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

I want to put on the record the statement that the minister is unable to provide that information.

That is what I have said.
Thank you.

These items have been going through so fast that I have not had a chance to ask the question I want to ask now. Can the minister make a statement as to subventions for maritime freight rates? Is enough provided to look after the twenty per cent increase in freight rates?
The answer is no.
That will be supplementary?
That is right.
Will the minister give an assurance that the twenty per cent over-all will be made available under the Duncan commission's freight rates recommendations?
It is statutory. It has to be done.

I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce, shortly after the freight rates were increased, Whether the subventions as applied to the movement of maritime coal would be increased to absorb the freight rate increase, and his answer was definitely, yes. It is merely a matter of stepping them up.
