speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Under this item I should like to ask the minister a question which no doubt he expects me to ask. I promise him I have no intention of repeating the speech-
Does my hon. friend promise it is the same question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, but I hope I get a different and better answer. My question has to do with government policy in relation to a transpacific air service. As the minister knows, in the past the stated policy of the government has been quite clear, namely that this service will be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines. Rumours that have appeared in the press, and the indefiniteness of ministerial answers have led me to wonder whether a

change, which I would deplore, is in prospect. Can the minister now state what is the present government policy with respect to the operation of a transpacific air service, particularly the service set out in the Canada-Australia agreement?

I am sorry I cannot enlighten the hon. member any more than I did the last time he asked the question. I have to repeat what I said then, namely, that the policy of the government has not been altered, and that if and when it is changed I shall make a statement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: About all I can say in reply to that is that it is just about the same amount of enlightenment as the minister gave previously, which is none. I hope there will be no change in government policy, but the kind of answers being given seem to suggest that one is in prospect; and it is, I fear, the sort of change I deplore and protest.

There is a matter I should like to bring before the minister under this item. I believe this is the correct item on which to do so ; if not I shall wait until later. I have had some correspondence with the Rivercrest community club; and for the information of the minister I may tell him this represents a new settlement of veterans' homes in my constituency. They are all in West St. Paul, and in this fully modern residential district there are fifty-eight veterans' homes. The whole district lies between the highway and the Red river. They are disturbed because an application has been made to the air transport board for a licence to operate an aircraft establishment, which would mean that planes would take off from and land on adjacent property. Perhaps I would save the time of the committee by quoting from the last letter I received, in which they say:
This not only constitutes a public nuisance and a hazard but decreases our property values also, and we are unanimously opposed to such an establishment in our neighbourhood. We petitioned against this undertaking to the municipal council, who passed a by-law prohibiting such installations within certain areas of the municipality and advised the Department of Transport of their action, requesting them at the same time to refuse to issue a licence. The Department of Transport here have referred the whole matter to Ottawa for decision, and we would like to have you intervene on our behalf if you would be kind enough to do so.
We are all greatly concerned over the matter, and several of our members have signified their intention of giving up their homes and moving elsewhere if the proposed aerodrome becomes a reality. We are building up a nice community here and rvould hate to see it spoiled.

Supply-T ransport
I do not think I can add very much to this. The veterans who have set up this modern residential district do not want an aerodrome next door if they can possibly avoid it. I appeal to the minister to have the air transport board give this matter every consideration.
I have to leave now for a meeting of the veterans affairs committee; if the minister is not able to give an answer at the moment, perhaps he could give one later.

All I can tell the hon. member now is that I am informed that if any such application has been made it is not to the knowledge of the board or the officers of the department. When such matters come before the board, licences are considered if in the public interest; and from the letter my hon. friend has quoted these representations unquestionably would be taken into consideration either by the board, if the letter should come before it, or the director of air services.
I can assure the hon. gentleman now that these representations will be brought to their attention.
Thank you very much. According to this letter the Winnipeg office has referred the whole matter to Ottawa; therefore it will probably come before the officials here.

I should like to bring the discussion back to the Pacific air routes. Am I to understand that no charter has been issued either to T.C.A. or any other applicant for the operation of Pacific air routes from Canada?

The answer is that no licence has been granted for transpacific services, either to T.C.A. or to any other carrier. In case I should be misunderstood, I should say a licence has been granted to an Australian company to operate a service from Australia to Canada, as the hon. gentleman knows.
But no Canadian company has yet received a reciprocal privilege?
No.

For a moment I should like to support the view that Canada should inaugurate Pacific flights from Canada, and should grant a Canada charter to a company to fly to the Pacific islands, Australia and New Zealand. In these times I think it imperative that we should open up such routes as these, even though in the beginning they may be a bit uneconomical to operate. I would urge that the government give every consideration to any application for such a charter, or to giving T.C.A. a charter to operate over those routes. I spoke on this matter in 1946, when
I was strongly of the opinion that we should draw the chains of empire closer together, and that Canada could perform a real service in opening up these routes to our sister commonwealths in the south Pacific.

Item agreed to.
Civil aviation division-
510.	Control of civil aviation, including the administration of the Aeronautics Act and regulations issued thereunder, $569,523.

There are several aeroplanes landing along the Red river under charters which permit them to operate ^ to various points in the northeastern portion of my constituency. They are rendering good service; but in landing on the Red river with their pontoons they cause considerable damage to the banks, which has led to several cave-ins, especially in the vicinity of the East Kildonan canoe club. I would ask the minister to see what can be done to keep these banks from falling in.
I shall be glad to look into the matter.

Item agreed to.
Civil aviation division-Airways and airports-
511.	Construction and improvements, including radio facilities; and to authorize commitments against future years in the amount of $452,000-capital, $11,138,309.
What radio installations are being made at airports controlled by the department, and where?
There is a long list of them.
I do not wish to delay the committee.
If the hon. member will say in which airport he is interested, I can give him the expenditures in respect of that one.
It would serve my purposes if the minister or his office would supply me with the information privately.
Thank you very much.

I have one further observation to make which I believe is of considerable importance. I wish to congratulate the minister's department upon having the foresight to employ Doctor Norman W. McLeod, whose contribution in runway construction has been unique. Doctor McLeod is a Canadian, and a graduate of Canadian universities. His contribution has been of a novel and excellent type, so much so that he was given an international award for his work, to which I shall refer briefly.
Supply-Transport

I believe Doctor McLeod is in the department on a part-time retainer basis; but his particular contribution is to bring to the technique of runway construction a new method of analysis of the undersoil, and a method of correlating the undersoil with the wheel loading which can be used on particular runways. His method can be applied not only to runway construction, but to any type of highway construction. When the results obtained by his method were compared with those of the United States corps of army engineers it was found that in some instances by his method it is necessary to use only about half or less than half the thickness of concrete in order to meet the safety factors required in runway construction.
I have taken these few minutes of the committee's time to congratulate the department upon having at its call such an excellent Canadian scientist who has made a real contribution to the development not only of our airways but of our highways as well.
Could the minister or his officials prepare a brief memorandum on this technique which could be passed on to all provincial departments and municipalities concerned with road building? This method represents a substantial saving to Canadian taxpayers. The application of his formula means a tremendous saving in public money in all fields of highway and air force runway construction.

Doctor McLeod has already prepared a report in the form of a book which deals with the very work to which the hon. member has referred, including preparation of the soil, and the like. We are making use of that book. While it is not a public document, it is in our possession, and if Doctor McLeod has no objection it could be circulated to the provincial governments.
I feel strongly it is the duty of the minister's department to see that this report has the widest possible circulation among those who are interested in construction work.

Before going to a special committee I should like to bring to the attention of the minister certain facts in connection with the airport at Castlegar in my constituency. It is now used principally by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. The airport is being maintained as a result of co-operation between the provincial government and the local citizens, and is providing excellent facilities.
The provincial government leased to the community a considerable area of land formerly owned by the Doukhobors. The local people have raised money and have done coasiderable work, so that they now have an 
airport fairly well advanced, and with possibilities for development into an excellent airport. This service is required in that part of the interior of British Columbia. In addition we have a number of smaller airports for the landing of smaller aircraft, which are coming into that district in increasing numbers, and for emergency landings. These airports have been neglected in recent years.
In view of the importance of the airport at Castlegar and the necessity for its development, I think it is most unfair that the development should rest with the local citizens. This airport serves a need in the community, and gives facilities for emergency landings. What is the government's policy with respect to these airports, and the giving of federal assistance for their development?

The policy is to help the airports on request. This airport is not under the jurisdiction of the department. It is operated and maintained by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. If application is made to the air transport board it will be dealt with in the same manner as other applications are handled.

Has the department
recently taken over from the R.C.A.F. the airport at. Patricia Bay?
Yes. We have taken it over for their operation, and for ourselves as well, and it is for their future use.
What about the administration of the airport?
It is our responsibility.

May I congratulate the minister upon having taken over such an excellent airport. For some time adjustments with neighbouring farmers in connection with the extension of runways and the establishment of guide poles have been somewhat up in the air. Now that the Department of Transport has taken over, can final settlement be speeded up? These farmers have been waiting for over twelve months for their adjustments. I am sure the minister's department knows the people to whom I refer. I would ask that since the department has now taken over, final settlement be made.
I can assure the hon. member that, having taken over, we will speed up adjustments as quickly as possible.
I have every confidence in the minister.

I should like to ask a general question about this group of items. I shall base my question on item 511, but I would point out that in

Supply-Transport
the group we have expenditures amounting to about $28,000,000. I should like to make this general observation: These are expenditures about which the ordinary layman can know very little. We are in the hands of the engineers, and we cannot expect the engineers to be particularly interested in money matters. I believe their whole instinct-and a very proper one indeed-is to try to carry their side of the matter as far as they can. Here we have expenditures which I suppose, according to judgment exercised, might vary between $10,000,000 and $15,000,000; they might run up to $40,000,000 or $50,000,000, according to the application of, first, construction, and second, the newest type of scientific investigation.
Obviously the minister cannot exercise complete and detailed judgment-and for two reasons: First, I believe it can be said he is not a technical man and, second, he is busy with other affairs. I should like to ask two questions. First of all, what means does the minister use to satisfy himself as to how far we should go? I admit that is a very difficult question, because in one way these new scientific inventions are useful and necessary, but in another way they are like delightful toys that people can play with ad lib. My second question is this: What is the relationship in matters of expenditure between the minister's department. as it applies to air transportation, and the Department of National Defence? I take it that scientific expenditures in respect of radio and the like are made under the air branch.

The hon. member asks what means are adopted to ascertain whether these expenditures are controlled. They are controlled in two ways: first, by the close watch which the treasury board keeps on all these items, and then by the air transport board to which application is made for additional services. In so far as the relationship between Defence and this department is concerned, anything of a civil nature is controlled entirely by the air division of transport. Some of the airports being abandoned by the Department of National Defence are taken over by us. I believe we took over last year some seventeen airports belonging to national defence and there is another item which we can discuss when we get to it if the hon. gentleman wishes.
Will part of this expenditure be made at Malton airport?
Yes.
Are Trans-Canada Air Lines charged for the use of Malton and other airports?
They pay landing fees and rental for hangars.
Where would that appear? Would that be in your budget?
It goes into consolidated revenue fund.
Approximately what are they paying for everything?
I am informed it is about $1,250,000.
That is in connection with all airports?
That is for all air services.
Is there an operating statement for Malton airport to show what the receipts and disbursements are?
Yes.
Can the minister give those figures?

A monthly report is received in connection with Malton airport showing the revenue and the expenditures. It is not a public document; it is for the information of the officers. I can see no objection, however, to getting the figures for the hon. gentleman if he wants them.

I do not want to press for figures which in themselves might not be significant, but it seems to me that it would be a matter of relevancy and of some importance to know in a general way what those reports showed, what revenue was produced and what were the carrying charges. I will not hold up the matter now. Perhaps the minister can give us the information later.
I notice in the breakdown given on page 279 an item of $1,817,000 for radio services. Can the minister give us some idea of how and where that is spent?

I was asked that question a moment ago, when I said there is a long list of items for radio services, which could be described pretty much as follows: 100 radio range stations, 15 fan markers, 3 frequency modulation relay stations, 11 instrument approach systems, and other installations with reference to radio in various airports. The list comprises some four or five pages. I can give the details if the hon. member wishes.

I do not think I want all the details. Will any of this money be spent at Malton? I was just wondering where it is spent and why.
Supply-Transport

There is no provision for radio construction at Malton, but there is for the installation of an instrument landing system, which is quite costly. Of the amount referred to in the estimates, $1,817,350 is being provided for radio services, with another $811,000 for the acquisition of radio equipment for various airports.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am interested in the point which has been pursued by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and the hon. member for High Park. I think the facts that they brought out are pertinent to the whole question of our air services. If I did not misunderstand them, they were getting at the fact that part of the cost of operating Trans-Canada Air Lines is hidden in these items covering airport and radio beam services. I think that is perfectly true. I should like to point out to them-and I think they will suspect what is coming-that the same thing applies to the privately-owned air lines. A while ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that it was only recently that private air lines such as the Canadian Pacific have been showing a profit. In order to be consistent, my hon. friends will have to admit that Canadian Pacific Air Lines show a profit only because many of the services necessary to the operation of their planes are paid for out of the public treasury.
The Canadian Pacific are operating their air services at a loss.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not want to follow what the hon. member of Muskoka-Ontario did last night, but that is not what your colleague told us not	long ago. He said	thatthey had got out of	the red	and	were	intothe black. Whether they are operating at a loss or a profit, the sums of money that we are voting right now are evidence that we are able to maintain air services in this country, whether privately or publicly owned, only because huge amounts of money are spent by the government in a capital way and on the operating of air services. I agree that this should be done, but	because	this	is in	thenature of a public	service	and	a public
monopoly, I have supported down through the years the extent to which the government has gone in for the public ownership and operation of air lines. I hope to see that policy continued, and not weakened or vitiated in any way by any backward step on the part of the government.

What is the present status of the Tofino airport? We spent about $5,000,000 there during the war and I am curious to know what the department is going to do with it.
[Mr. McMaster.J
It is maintained by the Department of Transport.

The
department is taking care of its upkeep?

And operation and
maintenance.

What is the situation with respect to the airstrip at Dawson Creek? The minister may not have the information at his fingers' ends, but I brought this to his attention some time ago. I do not even know at the moment under whose jurisdiction it comes, but I do know that it is badly in need of repairs, and I should like to know what the situation is.

I am informed that we have made a survey of the airport and airfield at Dawson Creek, and while no decision has yet been reached, it is a difficult operation and one that would be quite expensive to maintain. I would not like to go further at the moment.
( Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Transport a few questions in connection with item 511. In view of the stupendous development that has taken place in the northwestern part of the province of Quebec, it becomes important to set up an air line in that region. The minister has received numerous requests from different organizations of Val d'Or and Rouyn asking for the construction of airports. Our region has now a population of more than 100,000. Therefore it is essential that we give those people the opportunity of travelling a little more easily than they do now. By railway, the trip from Val d'Or to Montreal takes from 16 to 18 hours. So it is urgent to set up an air line.
Could the minister tell us whether he has received any petitions from Val d'Or or Rouyn with reference to the building of an airport at either place? What action has he taken in the matter? Do these credits provide for the building of an airport at the earliest opportunity?

Mr. Speaker, I may say that there has been no request for the building of an airport at Rouyn or Val d'Or, but there was one for the setting up of an air line, which is not quite the same thing. When the application is submitted to us formally-there are more than one, I am told-it will be acted upon in the regular way by the air transport board.

Supply-Transport
Were those applications for an air line charter filed by individuals or by companies.
Companies.
Privately owned companies?

Yes.
(Text):

I think the minister
should make a general statement on the construction of airfields. I do not want him to misunderstand me; I am not necessarily against them; in fact I am very much for them. But I think the committee is entitled to a statement in regard to the substantial expenditures which are being made, particularly in view of the fact, as has just been said, that Canadian Pacific Air Lines is losing money, and we also know that Trans-Canada Air Lines lost money last year, and we do not know just what the prospects are. As my colleague the member for Muskoka-Ontario said a short while ago, with most of the technical details in the hands of engineers, we may be doing things which are not a practical economic necessity. It is from this point of view that I would ask the minister to make a statement justifying these increases in expenditure. For example, item 511 shows that we appropriated last year $4,900,000, in round figures, and this year we are appropriating $11,138,000, an increase of approximately $6,200,000. We find in subsequent estimates that only a small portion of the total amount voted last year was used. I would like to know, first, why the amount voted last year was not used, and second, why the estimates this year exceed the total used and unused portions voted last year. In view of the fact that air lines in this country are operating at a loss, why are we making substantial appropriations to increase the facilities for something which does not justify itself economically?

The operation of these airports is of course being done at a loss. The house is familiar with the operations of T.C.A. It was operated at a profit for some years, but in the last two years there has been a deficit. That is the position not only in this country but in Great Britain and the United States; and in the United States the loss is proportionately greater than it is in Canada. The object of the department is to see that these airports are maintained in a condition that is safe for landing aircraft. What we do is to make the repairs, improvements and capital expenditures which are necessary in order to provide for the safety of the travelling public.
The item we are now discussing contains a revote of $3,109,500. The appropriation provides for the construction and improvement of airports, the construction and improvement of aerodromes and emergency landing fields to meet modem aviation requirements. It also provides for the installation of high intensity lighting, the extension of runways, boundary and approach lighting, the establishment and extension of radio facilities for the safe operation of airways in Canada and Newfoundland. The department has been fortunate in that many of the airports which were taken over were built during the war. If they had had to be built in peacetime the expenditure would have been not $11 million or more, but twice or perhaps three or four times as much. What we are doing now is to maintain and operate them for the safety of air navigation.

Where is the end of these large expenditures, as well as of current maintenance expenditures, in this particular field? Is it the view of the government that these air services will ever justify themselves from a dollar-and-cents point of view? If the minister replies in the negative, that in the foreseeable future the revenues from these air services will not equal the expenditures, should not these airports and facilities be looked upon as a matter of national defence and not as something having to do with civil aviation?
I hope the day will come when these services will pay for themselves. But, as my hon. friend has intimated, I cannot say that that is possible in the near future.

Substantial reconstruction is under way at Malton airport. What amount does this item provide for the reconstruction of buildings and for control and other improvements of the field at Malton? Is anything provided here for the Toronto island airport? Is any extension contemplated by the department which will increase the usefulness of the island airport, or is it simply to be used in the future as it has up to the present, largely for small planes and trainers? Are any changes contemplated at the Uplands airport? I understand that since the new planes were introduced by Trans-Canada Air Lines they are not using the Uplands airport. Apparently the field at Uplands is not large enough for the new planes that are in service; they are operating directly between Montreal and Toronto, but not on the triangular service via Uplands. Can the minister tell us something about that, and indicate whether any changes are provided for Uplands under this item?

There is provision for extending the runways at the Malton airport.
Supply-Transport

As my hon. friend knows, a substantial sum is being expended for renovation of the administration building.

How much?
Mr. CH'EVRIER: I will get the figure in a minute. We are not spending any money on the island airport. It is under the jurisdiction of the Toronto harbour commissioners. At Uplands, or the Ottawa airport, we do not propose to make the runways large enough to accommodate the new T.C.A. North Stars. We feel that that expenditure would not be justified at the moment.
Can the minister give the expenditures at Malton under this item?
They are provided in another item. The amount for the completion of the terminal building, facilities and administration building at Malton is $525,000.
When is it expected to be completed?
When I saw it two weeks ago it was progressing fairly well. I would think that by the end of August or early September it would be completed.

Who is responsible for making requests for improvements at the various airports? They must come from somebody. When requests do come in, on what basis is it decided whether the expenditure should be made or not?

The demand for improvements is made by the district inspector, and they are given consideration by the director of air services, who decides in the affirmative or in the negative in accordance with the importance of the airport, the amount of traffic, and the economic need.
Do the inspectors get their information or requests from the various air lines such as the T.C A., the C.P.A., the United States lines, and so on, which are using these fields?

If my hon. friend has Malton in mind, the inspector is in Toronto. Toronto is the headquarters of the central division. He would be guided by the amount of traffic and also by the representations that were made to him by the various air lines using the port.

The air lines are the one who really make the request. We have been talking about operations. Is there a standard schedule of charges for the various air lines? What are these charges? Are they the same in Canada as they are in the United

States for similar airports, and do all the air lines pay the same charges? What is the total revenue that comes in by way of charges? I should like to know how the charges compare.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would it be better to let these questions stand until we reach the item?
The discussion has been very general on this item. We have been going on to other items. I shall try to get the information for my hon. friend.

I want to know what the charges are and whether they should be higher or lower. The government does not own railway stations; the railways have to put them up themselves. It seems to me that the air lines which are operating should pay an economic rent for the stations they use.

The charges that my hon. friend inquired about are uniform throughout the country. They are not necessarily the same in this country as they are in the United States. They are based on the economic service.
Are our charges lower or higher than the charges of comparable airports in the United States?

I am informed that we cannot compare the charges in this country with those of the United States, because they are not based on the same service. The rates and the charges are not established on the same basis.

There are two air lines operating from Toronto to New York. One is operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines and the other by a United States air line. Do these lines pay the same charges at Malton near Toronto as they pay in New York when they land there? Is there a difference, and if so, why? Why should we charge less than they do, if we do?

The United States has no standard basis for the establishment of these charges. They vary in each state, and sometimes at each airport. That is why it is difficult to compare them. In some instances ours are higher and in others they are lower, but in every instance there is uniformity throughout the country.
Do we pay the same landing charges at LaGuardia field in New York as the United States air lines do? Do the United States air lines pay the same charges at Malton as Trans-Canada Air Lines pay?

There is no discrimination at any airport as to the amount of the charges.

Supply-Transport
Does Trans-Ganada pay the same charges in New York as the United States air lines pay?
Yes.

Here we are contemplating an expenditure of about $30,000,000. I ask the minister this question. Are we just going along doing this, that and the other thing, which we think is important, partly for civil aviation and partly for military aviation? Is there any plan of any kind in our minds? In the first place, is there any reason why we should carry commercial passengers at away below cost? I assume wre are doing that. If I am wrong, the minister will correct me; if I am right, why are we doing it? What basis is there for arriving at this huge expenditure? Here are millions of dollars to be spent on airports. I imagine it is fully justified, but I do not know. There may be justification purely from the national defence point of view, but I think the minister should give us a statement indicating some underlying principles. We are engaged here in the completely blind business of voting millions of dollars in the absence of any principle on which the money is being spent, and in particular-I come back to this-without knowing whether those who are using the air purely as a means of transport, without any particular reason, are paying their way. In charter services, such as the bush lines, the lines up in Muskoka, and the tourist resorts, people must pay their own way. They do not get government assistance, and I do not think they should; but I suggest that people using the air for ordinary travel should not get government assistance either.
I come back to the first question. Must there not be in the government's mind some basis whereon they determine whether they shall spend ten, twenty, thirty or forty millions, and must there not be in their mind also some part of that amount which is necessary for the purpose of national defence and which would have to be spent anyway? Can we be given that figure? Can we, in other words, be put in a position to exercise some kind of judgment? At the moment all we can do is look at the amount of money we are spending, without knowing the principle on which it is spent.
The request is a legitimate one, and I think the best I can do is to prepare a statement, which I will bring in as quickly as possible, outlining the reasons and the basis for the expenditure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before any other hon. member speaks, may I say to the committee
that I try to see that discussion comes from every quarter of the chamber and is not confined to any particular party or group. With that object in mind, it is perhaps necessary for me to call on an hon. member who has stood up only once, when some other hon. member may have stood up four or five times in an effort to get the floor. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has the floor now.

I am curious to know whether the department has been approached by any of the air lines operating in Canada, in the same manner as the steamship lines have approached him, and approached him so successfully. If we give them $2,000,000 in the form of a subsidy to serve people in the outlying areas, has his department considered the granting of subsidies to bush air lines? Coming to the Post Office Department, one can establish an excellent case for the provision of air-mail service. The people in some parts of my riding receive mail every ten or twelve days, and it is conceded down here that that is not good enough, but they say that they are not the department of government which has the function of subsidizing air services. The time is coming when the departments of transport and reconstruction will have to face the problem of providing assistance or better facilities for the people who live on the frontiers. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario suggested that the government should not give assistance. I hope I do not misunderstand him. His riding and mine are similar in certain respects. I suggest that if Canada is to be developed, the people who live in the cities, enjoying all the facilities that are provided, must see to it that the people who live on the frontiers and who are producing the natural wealth of the country are also provided with these facilities. I should be glad to assist the minister with my humble vote if he ever came here with provision for assisting the bush-flying organizations. I do not know whether Canadian Pacific Air Lines on the main routes or Trans-Canada need great assistance, apart from what they get now in the provision of first class airports; but these airports, apart from their military value, strike me as being much the same as government docks that we provide. They are for the service of all the people. Heaven knows when any of us will have to use the lines for very urgent reasons. There must be some way in which the department can be of assistance to the people in the outlying districts. I am all for it.

Perhaps the day will come when we shall have to consider the
Supply-Transport

question of subsidies to air lines and air carriers. Thus far we have not given it consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Except indirectly.
My hon. friend has taken the words out of my mouth. We have done so indirectly by aiding in the construction of airports and aerodromes, and paying for their operation and maintenance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And radio beam services.
That is right.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni made an excellent socialist speech a moment ago.

I am
broadminded.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He comes from British Columbia.

I do not need to repeat what he said. However, I wish to ask a question. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and others have criticized these expenditures. They wish to know whether they have justified or will justify themselves. I believe they have done so already. In Trans-Canada Air Lines the people of Canada have something to be proud of.
Hear, hear.

I think that if we ever arrive at the point at which the hon. member is aiming, where we shall have a fair base to work from and supervise service in the air, there will have to be a consolidation of all under one government department. In my opinion this form of travel, so far as the public is concerned, will have to be closely supervised, and I do not think there is anyone in the country in a position to do that job except the government of Canada, which is responsible to the people. In my opinion the bush lines and C.P.A. should be under T.C.A. There is no comparison between the services, and if the job is to be done properly the government now is providing practically all the facilities. The other lines get the benefit of it. The time will come when the whole thing will have to be operated by the government; I have no doubt about that. What I did rise to ask the minister-
You were going to ask a question.
You do not like what I am saying, do you?

He didn't say that.
Maybe you would like him to.
You are willing that they should spend all the money.

If you have been reading the newspapers and watching the trend of events in the country within the last few months you will come to that conclusion too. You cannot hold the tide back.
I challenge contradiction of the statement a3 to the comparison of the services. The one service in Canada that I am proud of is T.C.A. They are doing an excellent job, and I do not think we are good Canadians if we do not admit it. Every dollar spent on T.C.A. has been money well spent. There are many other things we are spending money on for which we are not getting value.
I will put my question. During the war there was a meteorological service at Sydney airport. It is the main jumping-off point for overseas airways and the main landing point on the way back. That service was discontinued. I understand that they must get weather reports from other places, and that delays them and causes confusion at times. Is there any intention of re-establishing the service there? I think it is absolutely necessary. Further, to what extent is the department encouraging the development of civil aviation at that airport at Sydney? I know a small commercial company was formed there to give service to outlying sections, with small planes, and I believe they were having considerable difficulty in reaching an understanding with the department.

The answer to the first question would be yes, that the meteorological services at Sydney are now in the process of being re-established. As far as the importance of the airport is concerned, there can be no doubt about that. It is not, of course, the only important one. Dorval is the most important, in the sense that it is a transatlantic airport; but Sydney is being given consideration as an alternate.

Is any part of this amount of $11,138,000 for the construction and improvement of airports earmarked for the Clover Valley airport near Saint John? A few years ago the then minister of transport gave the municipality the green light to go ahead and acquire land with a view to the establishment of an airport there. The municipality went ahead and expropriated the land; then the matter was held up. Is the minister able to tell us the present position with respect to that proposed airport, and whether any of this money is to be used to develop it?
I should like also to ask the minister whether any portion of this amount is earmarked for

Supply-Transport
the purpose of developing an airport at or near Fredericton, New Brunswick. Last September and October there was a great deal of discussion in some parts of New Brunswick as to the development of an airport at Fredericton. Will the minister tell us whether any of this money is to be used for that purpose, and whether it is the intention of the government to go ahead with an airport at the capital city of the province?

There is no provision in these estimates for the construction or extension of an airport at either Saint John or Fredericton. Pennfield Ridge, which is an ex-R.C.A.F. airport thirty or thirty-five miles from Saint John, is being used by and for the people of that city.
Could the minister develop the point any further at the moment, as to whether anything is being done to provide Fredericton with an airport?
I cannot, at this stage.

Is the minister able to say whether anything more is being done in connection with the airport at Clover Valley, near Saint John? Is that matter still in mind, or has the government decided to wash out the whole thing?
No decision has been arrived at as yet.
In either case?
I have given the answer with respect to Fredericton; I said I was not able to give any information. I shall do so when the supplementaries are up for discussion.
Then may I ask the minister if there will be any estimates in the supplementaries for the Fredericton airport?
I do not know.

I do not often go to New Brunswick, but it is always a great pleasure when I do. Last fall I was there on some public business, and at that time a great many things were said about an airport for Fredericton. It seemed suspiciously close to by-election time, and I was wondering if perhaps the government promises were to be carried out in the supplementary estimates.
I did not make the promises; I do not know what they were.
I did not find the minister there, but there were plenty of others ready to speak on his behalf.
Is there no cabinet solidarity in the matter of election promises?

I am sorry, but I do not think the minister answered one of my questions. I want to know the charges when one of our planes lands at LaGuardia field, whether they are the same as the charges at Malton. I should like a comparison.
The answer is no.
Then what is the difference between the cost of landing at LaGuardia field and landing at Malton?
It would depend on the size of the aircraft and the schedule.
Take the regular trans-Canada plane that goes from here and lands at LaGuardia field. How much do they charge us? Then take the same plane coming back to Malton. How much is it charged there?
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit me to answer the question by sending him a copy of the tariff. It is pretty lengthy and a somewhat complicated document.
Surely the minister can answer that simple question.
I have not the tariff before me.
I should like to know the difference.
I shall be glad to get the tariff and send it to my hon. friend as quickly as possible.

Very well.
Then, following the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, what are the prospects of these airports becoming what might be called economic in their operation? When may we expect expenditures to go down and revenues to come up? Is there any prospect of that? From the information we have obtained today, and in view of this amount of something like 88 million for operating expenses alone, it seems to me that we are voting one of two things. I should like to know if we are voting something that is necessary for Canada, or whether we are voting an expensive luxury. It seems to me that is the way to put it, because I have not been able to make up my mind which it is. We have a great many boards to look after. We are told this [DOT] board does this and that board does that, and the recommendations come in. I do not know how well they are supervised; I do not know how necessary they are, and as yet the minister has not told us how necessary all these things may be.
Supply-Transport

I promised the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that I would bring in a statement setting out the basis. In reply to the specific question my hon. friend asks, namely, as to the chances of these airports becoming economic in their operation, I stated a moment ago that in the foreseeable future I could not see that they would become so, though eventually I hope they will. All I can say is that the gap is gradually closing.

I want to make a plea to the minister with respect to a specific airstrip, namely the one at Banff. This is a small strip in the centre of one of our national parks, where service is provided by a small operator named Gaetz, who is doing some excellent pioneer work in flying in the Rocky mountains. This service is making great areas of the Rockies available to people who otherwise could not possibly see them, without engaging expensive pack trains and having expensive equipment. Service from this strip is opening up a vast mountain territory which up to the present has been virtually unknown to and unseen by Canadians and Americans alike. I realize that in the national parks there are certain restrictions with respect to flying, which in the main I think are archaic; but if for no other reason than that of dollars and cents, in attracting United States tourists, I should like to see this airstrip provided with shelter, facilities for tethering light aircraft, a hangar, and gasoline service. It is estimated that today in the United States there are about 300,000 owners of private aircraft. Most of these are light machines, and the owners do a considerable amount of touring and travelling. I believe that if this airstrip were made available to owners who wish to take a flying holiday, it would be of great advantage to Canada.
I have flown there myself. I have flown out of Banff and extensively around the Rockies. I believe it can be said there is nowhere else in the world where one would find such magnificent scenery or a territory which might be opened up with such profit as our own Rocky mountain region. This is particularly so in the winter months when, because of the vast snowfields, landing hazards are greatly diminished.
I believe the airport itself could be of great value, not only to open up the vast mountain areas, but as a great revenue producer from Americans who wish to come here with their own aircraft in the summer months.

We are not doing a great deal in connection with the development of the airstrip at Banff. The same applies to Jasper. The reason is that the landing field is
rMr. Ross (St. Paul's).]
on national parks' property, and the parks administration is opposed in principle to the extensive development of those resort areas. Then, while the country is all right to fly over, it is not easy to land in. So that at the present time we are not contemplating any expenditures at Banff.

I realize the difficulties and I understand that attitude of the parks branch. I believe I have said before that it is archaic. I have done considerable flying in the national parks, and I know that, particularly in the winter months, the difficulties of landing are not as great as have been emphasized. I believe aircraft, and particularly the light variety, offer one of the few ways of really opening up the national parks.
When this matter is considered between the minister himself and the Minister of Mines and Resources, who has direction of the national parks, I hope consideration will be given to the tremendous advantage of making the national parks available to the people. At the present time eighty or ninety per cent of national park areas are not available, unless those who wish to go there outfit themselves with expensive pack trains or are prepared to go on major mountaineering expeditions, either of which is extremely costly. By means of aircraft, great areas of the national parks are made available to the man of average means.

Surely the hon. member for York West does not mean that, by the use of air transportation, the parks will become available to persons of average means. Either they won't or his "person of average means" must have means considerably above what I consider average. [DOT] I think of my own constituency of Vancouver East, composed of average people-ordinary people, people who work in factories and stores.
In Russia they live in palaces.

Some do; and in this country also, some people live in palaces. Perhaps the situation has not changed at all; except that different people are living in the palaces today than lived in them in the past.
But that is not what I am looking for- although it is what my hon. friend is afraid might happen. He is afraid there might be a change here in those who are living in the palaces today. I am thinking of the people who find it all they can do to take their children to the park on a Sunday afternoon or on a holiday-and travel by street car. These are the average people in Canada; and they do not go either by aeroplane or by pack train to our national parks.

Supply-Transport
I do not think any great claim can be made for the development of airstrips in our national parks. There is a great deal of development of civil aviation still to be done in Canada, and I shall be prepared to support the minister in that part of the development which is economically useful and reasonable.
Could we get back to a consideration of the specific details in the vote? What are the seventeen airports the minister took over last year?
There is a specific item for that later on, at which time I shall give the details.
Is any portion of the $11,000,000 being voted for the development of new types of engines and experimental aircraft?
No.
Where does that item come in?
There is no such item.
Do I understand that the dominion government has no interest in the experimental work going on at Malton airport?

Yes, we have a deep interest-but not in this department. The Department of Reconstruction and Supply did spend a considerable amount of money on the development of aircraft engines and equipment. What the position is today in so far as their expenditures are concerned, I do not know. All I can say is that there is no provision in these estimates for that item.

Does this amount of $11,000,000 represent more in the way of an initial outlay than a final or complete outlay for equipment for the air force for the supply of radio ranges and instrument Landing equipment?

It is neither the initial nor the final; this is a continuing item. I belie.ve I shall be able to establish, when I answer the question asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, that we look at these airports across the country and decide how much it is possible to spend this year. Then we apportion it in accordance with the needs, safety and importance of the airport or aerodrome.

I have had some experience with these matters and I know how costly it is. If Canada wishes to retain any place in the aviation field the government will have to be prepared to make these expenditures.

No doubt some of the expenditures will be for lengthening and
strengthening runways to accommodate the four-engine North Star aircraft? I understand that a jet transport plane is now being developed. If it is accepted, as it gives every promise of being, will the runways have to be strengthened or lengthened? Would the minister be good enough to say whether or not that consideration has been borne in mind in these appropriations?
I am informed by the director of air services that the jet transport plane, as now being developed, will take about the same size of runway as the North Star.
I understood, on what I believe was good authority-I know nothing about the technical details-that a jet-operated plane will not require as long a runway or as heavy a roadbed. Is that the fact?
It will require about the same strength of runway, but the length has not been determined.
Will any substantial part of vote oil be used to lengthen runways to accommodate the new four-engine planes we are using?
No.

This seems to be a case of the blind leading the blind. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has said he is in accord with the manner in which this government enterprise is being carried on. The facts have shown quite clearly in the last three months that private corporations are able to run in the black rather than in the red, but he claims that they should be taken over by the government. I think he is trying to mislead this committee and the people of Canada when he advocates taking over Canadian Pacific Air Lines and other similar companies that have [DOT]been able to operate without any assistance from the taxpayers. The Canadian Pacific have gone ahead on their own under private enterprise and are now operating at a profit. It is certainly a case of the blind leading the blind-they have been partly successful in the last three months-and the people will soon get on to that kind of nonsense. I think we are doing a great job of squandering the taxpayers' money. The fact is that the hon. gentleman knows nothing about aviation in any way, shape or form.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member for Sim-coe North says that private companies like the Canadian Pacific do not ask for a single dollar of the taxpayers' money. He makes that statement right at the moment this committee is voting $11 million, along with other items, to provide for air services which the minister
Supply-Transport

admitted a while ago constitute indirect assistance to all companies, including private air lines such as the Canadian Pacific.
May I say this to the hon. member who has resumed his seat: Has not the Canadian Pacific railroad assisted the government railroad just as much as this? It is not all charity from- the government.

Item agreed to.
Civil aviation division-
515. Grants to organizations for the development of civil aviation, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $30,000.

I want to say something in connection with the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association. I note in thie details relating to item 515 there is a grant to the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association of $5,000, and it is upon that item I desire to say a word or two. No doubt members of parliament generally have, from time to time, been kept in touch by the organization known as the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association with the financial aspect of the association's activities. As the minister knows and the committee is aware, prior to the war, indeed as early as 1928, a flying clubs association was set up, comprising the operators of flying clubs throughout Canada, and until the war broke out, government grants were made to each of these clubs. If my memory serves me aright, there was at one time a grant of $1,000 to each of these clubs from the dominion treasury. It requires no words of mine, Mr. Chairman, to indicate the vital importance of the work done and the contributions made by those who were trained in the flying clubs of this country prior to 1939. Some 350 pilots, properly trained, were available at the time war broke out. Many others had gone overseas prior to 1939 and enlisted in the Royal Air Force. The importance of the work done by these flying clubs therefore does not need to be -emphasized at this time, because it is generally recognized and is well known to all hon. members. But with the war the activities of these clubs were diverted, of course, to other things, and not until after the war was over did the old flying clubs attempt to re-establish themselves and new clubs come into being.
One of my personal interests in this matter is the excellent and progressive flying club which has been established in my own part of Canada near the town of Brampton. I think most of us realize what this means with respect to our whole national picture. There are at the present time some forty-three flying clubs in the organization known as the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association.
Training pilots has never been a profitable business; it has been an unprofitable business by and large, and I am told that none of these
clubs all across Canada is in a strong financial position, but rather that most of them can be said to be in a weak financial position, with some of them running definitely in the red. I do not need to emphasize to this committee or to the minister or the government how important flying training is to our national defence, or the other aspects of the club's activities which, of course, are valuable assets in peacetime set-up. Bearing that in mind, it seems to me-that the government should include in its estimates a grant or subsidy to these flying clubs. I know of nothing that would meet with more general approval, and I make an earnest plea to the minister now to see if that cannot be done before the session is brought to a close. It may be that the minister has in mind including an amount for that purpose in the supplementary estimates, and if so I hope that it will be a generous amount, because the young men who are operating the flying clubs are for the most part veterans who gave conspicuous service to their country in the recent war. They are trying now in another way to do something for Canada in peace, and perhaps also have in mind our national security in case of another emergency. I think, therefore, it becomes a matter of national concern. I should not like to see club after club go out of existence, simply because the government had not given them something in the way of the grant which they required.
The operational costs of these clubs have, of course, increased as have the operational costs of everything else. The clubs are confined, as you, Mr. Chairman, well know, to certain kinds of training, and they have not the opportunities of going into commercial business as some other concerns have whereby they can make a profit which helps to keep the other end of their operations out of the red. I hope that the minister will be sympathetic to the plea I am making on behalf of a section of our citizens who have done a magnificent job in war and are anxious to do a similar job in peace, through training young men in the art and science of flying. I would ask the minister to give every possible consideration to the plea I have just made.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that I have some knowledge of the work done by these clubs, because when I was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply I had the good fortune to be chairman of a subcommittee which went into this matter thoroughly and strongly recommended in favour of assistance being given to these clubs. In fact, I think the report went so far as to say that if it had not been for the
Supply-Transport

work of the flying clubs it would have been impossible to develop our air strength to the position it reached. The hon. gentleman will find me quite sympathetic to the application that has already been made. I have had the responsibility for this part of the Department of Transport for about a month. One of the first things that came to my attention then was this very matter to which my hon. friend refers. I have not been able to deal with it in the sense of arriving at a decision, but I can assure him that it will be given careful and most sympathetic consideration.
In this item $5,000 is provided for the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association. That, of course, does not begin to meet the position. It is a grant which is included in the estimates. When the time comes for consideration of the supplementary estimates I think I would be prepared to see that a similar amount is put in the supplementaries; but on the general question raised, I can tell the hon. member now that he will find me sympathetically disposed toward it.	*
May I make one suggestion. I think something more than another $5,000 would be in order-
I agree.
-because that would seem to me to be wholly inadequate. I believe the minister will agree with me that something much more substantial than that will be necessary to alleviate the present situation.

I did not intend to leave the impression that a grant of $5,000 or even S10,000 would meet the situation. Neither did I want to leave the impression that the problem can be dealt with in the supplementary estimates. I do not think it can be, but I can assure the hon. member that it will be carefully looked into.

I want to add a word. Some two months ago I made reference to this matter in the house. I think it was on the speech from the throne that I brought the matter to the attention of the minister. I do not believe the present minister was charged with that branch of the department at that time. When I saw these estimates I came to the conclusion that, in making an appeal for more consideration, I was just a voice crying in the wilderness. I mentioned at that time that civilian groups put large amounts of capital into the picture. At that time the flying clubs associations across Canada took hold of the promotion of the training of aviators so urgently needed at the beginning of the war.
When the minister mentions $5,000 I know
it is just a nominal amount. He has shown us

that he is sympathetic. The committee appreciates that, but I wish to remind the minister of the work done, not only by the personnel of the flying clubs associations, but by the great men who got behind this with their money. We do not know just how soon we may have to turn to these facilities again. In these days of uncertainty we never know what will happen. When the minister comes to make his decision I hope that he will put a couple of digits at the end of the $5,000.

I should like to support the stand that 'has been taken by the hon. member for Peel and the hon. member for Lincoln in requesting assistance for the flying clubs of Canada. In doing so, I shall not go into the job that they did before and during the war, except to say that they formed the elementary flying training schools which turned out the bulk of the British commonwealth air training plan pilots. As the minister knows, at the end of the war they turned back millions of dollars-I am prompted to say $6,000,000-to the government. It would be unfair if I did not point out the situation which has arisen as a result of some of the government's kindness to these clubs. Although they turned back their money, the government did hand over to them hangars and many other facilities at these various airports. We now find that the cost of operation and maintenance of the very things that were given to them has placed some of the clubs in an unfortunate position. We cannot criticize the government for what it has done. We can say that in many instances the clubs have taken, on more than they can handle. I suggest to the minister that the government consider permitting the clubs to draw on the moneys turned back at the end of the war for the training of pilots to licensed standards. I would say men and women pilots, because I do not think women should be excluded from the aviation field.
Of course we can turn to the defence side of the picture and make a good case for it there, but even on the civil side of it there is no doubt that our country is peculiar in the way in which it lends itself to all forms of aviation, geographically and in many other ways. Unless we develop pilots, we shall never be able to explore, settle or progress to the north in the way that we should. The moneys that were handed back could be used for this, and I am sure the minister could make a good case before his colleagues.
I was pleased to hear him say this afternoon that he had had an initial experience with these clubs. I am sure that his dealings

with them will have convinced him, as they have convinced me, from what I have seen of them, that at least they are run by excellent citizens, people with vision and imagination, people who, if given some assistance now, could continue to do the wonderful job for our country that they have in the past.
I shall end as I have begun by asking the minister for more than the sympathetic support of his colleagues. I ask him to put the case to them before the supplementary estimates are brought down, so that this temporary pre-war scheme can be reinstated and the whole position fully discussed between the government and the flying clubs.

How many of these meteorological stations are there in Canada and what is the set-up? Some in the north country have only one man. Can the minister let us know something about the department in which we spend so much money?

There are about twelve main forecast offices in such places as Goose, Gander, Halifax, Moncton, Dorval, Malton, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Whitehorse and Vancouver, and 220 surface weather reporting stations. Of these, 110 provide weather information every hour and thirty-five provide winds aloft information.
Most of those in the north are the kind with only one man?

The surface weather stations would have from two to four, and the main forecast offices would have as many as forty. There are 740 climatological stations. Of these, about 460 are manned by voluntary observers.

Two years ago the forecast station at Victoria was discontinued and, since then, we have been getting weather reports from Vancouver. It would appear that the weather on the south coast of Vancouver island has deteriorated ever since that change. Can we get our station back?-because really there has been no change in the weather.

Mr. SiKEY: What is the division of responsibility as between the minister and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply? Are all these items which we have dealt with this afternoon under the immediate jurisdiction and authority of the Minister of Transport?

Recently I had an opportunity of seeing it in operation, and I was tremendously impressed with the clarity with which the picture comes through on, the electronic beam and tube. I should like to put on record one or two statistics for the minister's consideration. There are twenty-seven television broadcasting stations now in operation, and there will be a coast to coast hook-up in the United States by the end of this year.

Air service-Radio division-
519. Suppression of radio interferences, $321,281.

Under this item, I want to bring two matters to the attention of the minister, one concerning radio reception in my district, and the other having to do with radio interference. In the district I have the honour to represent, wre have two radio stations, one at Trail and the other at Nelson. I speak of the situation there, because I know' in recent years these stations have served the outlying districts less and less, as a result of the increased power of the United States stations. The local stations serve the two communities of Trail and Nelson very well indeed, but in the upper portion of the Arrow lakes, particularly, and in some parts of the Kootenay lakes these stations cannot be heard satisfactorily, particularly at night. I am not an expert; I have very little knowledge of anything mechanical; but cannot something be done by putting in a booster station, or something of that sort, to provide satisfactory radio reception for those living in these isolated places? I realize it is a difficult problem, but quite a large number of my constituents now get very poor reception indeed, which I understand is largely due to the fact that the stronger United States stations drown out the local stations, particularly during the evening hours.
There is another point with respect to radio interference. It seems that as the years go by, interference becomes worse and worse. I understand that all the new electrical gadgets,
Supply-Transport

razors and machines of all types, cause a great deal of difficulty. I believe the departmental officials have toured the district and done their best to locate the trouble; but it is still a serious matter, so much so that in the upper Arrow lakes and some sections of the Kootenay lakes it is not worthwhile to listen to the radio. I do not know what the laws are in that respect; but I am sure something can be done to place protective devices on this electrical equipment, which is being used to a far greater extent than ever before; and this must be done if we are to have any sort of satisfactory radio reception.
I should like the minister's comments on the matter of reception and on the question of radio interference.

If the poor reception to which the hon. member refers is due exclusively to other, high-powered stations either in our own country or in another country, then the way to overcome that difficulty is for the private station to increase its power. That situation did not exist years ago, when many stations both in Canada and the United States used less power than they use today. The situation in my hon. friend's community is a duplication of what is happening elsewhere. Many of the smaller stations have found it necessary to make application for an increase in power, and in most cases, when the position is as my hon. friend states, these applications have been granted.
As far as interference is concerned, we have inspectors looking after such matters. I do not know where the nearest one would be to my hon. friend's constituency; I presume he would be in Vancouver, though I am not too sure. It is part of the duties of these inspectors to go out with the interference car and ascertain what may be the cause of the bad reception. There is a multitude of causes, such as defective wiring or alternate current.
\ ery often in the homes there are oil burners, washing machines and the like which affect the reception. If the hon. member will write to the inspector or say a word to the officers I think there would be no question about the inspector's going out, getting the facts and finding out what the causes are, with a view to eliminating them. Some of those causes are local, and sometimes people do not like to instal the equipment necessary to do away with the interference.

[Air. Herridge.]
think I would like to see the C.B.C. in the capable hands of the Minister of Transport. The two would work well together.

Perhaps the best answer to the question would 'be this, that if the radio service were under the C.B.C. or if the C.B.C. were under the radio service branch of this department, that would meet the position. It has
always seemed to me that the Department of National Revenue could have nothing to do with radio. Certainly there is no revenue from the C.B.C. It would seem to me much more satisfactory to have it in the hands of the minister.

The hon. member for Mackenzie and I have had communications in the last two years in which we have pointed out radio interference at Gillam, Wabowden and Churchill, caused by the operation of government teletype machines at Churchill. Mr. Chairman, to my mind the C.B.C. should be under the wing of the Department of Transport. This vote shows extravagance on the part of the government, and there can be no justification for the vote at all. It is just a silly thing. This is a nuisance tax, and we find that the consolidated

Supply-Transport
revenue fund has to pay for the collection of this 12.50 tax, the amount of the licence fee.
The C.B.C. receives the full amount of fees collected. The situation is really incongruous. It is hard to understand how the government would act in this way. Here we have an expenditure of $571,439 to collect $4,798,000. I got those figures today from the C.B.C., and perhaps the minister would tell me if they are correct. This $571,439 is not chicken-feed; it is taken from the taxpayers of this country, just in the same way as any other taxing money comes from the taxpayers. This amount of money appearing in the vote is the expense in connection with the collection of moneys to be paid over to the C.B.C. It is raised by the Department of National Revenue, through taxation of one kind or another which, on the average, is collected for about one per cent. But when one looks at this he finds the ridiculous situation where it costs eleven per cent to collect this sum of $4,798,000 which is paid over to the C.B.C. I cannot understand how anyone with ordinary common sense would say that we should pay eleven per cent to collect a nuisance tax; and why it is collected, I do not know. Why pay that amount, when money can be collected for slightly more than one per cent?
More than that, many people forget to pay this tax, and other people do not buy licences. There are plenty of people who have radios and who have paid no tax.
Not only that, if you have one radio you must pay a tax of $2.50, but if you have ten radios you pay no more. However, if you have a radio in your car you must pay $2.50 extra. The whole thing is silly. And if one does not pay his tax, the next thing he knows he is hauled into court and must pay not only the tax but the expense of collecting it, and a fine.
Why is the tax collected? It is collected, supposedly, to support the C.B.C. in its programming. Yet, in many places the C.B.C. cannot be heard. Only a short time ago in Fort Frances, while the C.B.C. could not be heard, the people were forced to pay their tax, simply because they had radios.
This amount is not for the policing of radio, because that is provided for in another vote. The Department of Transport does that on another basis by an expenditure from the consolidated revenue fund. This $571,439 is simply for the collection of the $2.50 fee from everyone. It is collected from the pensioner who gets only $40 a month, from the burnt-out soldier, from the widows-and to these people the expenditure means a great deal. The whole thing is ridiculous.
And, what is worse, it is not the listener who must pay, but the owner of the radio. It is he
who pays the sales tax, the 25 per cent luxury tax; and because he has a radio operating he must pay this fee of $2.50. The whole thing is so silly! I cannot say how silly I think it is! What the principle is I do not know. If you are going to tax at all, you should tax every radio. On the other hand, if you are going to tax you ought to tax the people who are listening, not the people who have the radio and are giving enjoyment to the public who have no radio.
I just have to make this protest again. I could go on and talk much longer. Parliament passed an act which provided that the C.B.C. were not to be charged for the collection of this fee as had been the case in the past. All you need to do if the C.B.C. needs money is to pay them something for every person in Canada, pay them on a per capita basis and have them stick to that, instead of having this nuisance tax, having people come up and ring your doorbell and ask if you have paid your radio fee. There are hundreds of other people who have not and others are called into court because they have not paid or have neglected to pay. The thing is just too silly when one comes to think of it.
It costs $571,439 to collect $4,798,000 which the C.B.C. get without any charge. Why should they get the total amount? It is only a subterfuge. If they need more money, why not raise the rates, or why not charge on every radio?
If this is an indication of government policy in connection with the estimates of the other departments; if all estimates are as extravagant as this, then we ought to scrutinize the estimates of all the departments much more than we have been doing. This $571,439 is the taxpayers' money, and it is collected for no reason at all that I can see.

This item reads:
Issue of radio receiving licences-(Transport department only).
What other cost is there in the issuing of radio licences if this does not cover it all?
There are accounting services by the Department of Transport.

In going through the minister's estimates, I find that over three-quarters of a million dollars are for sundry items. Surely there should be a better system of handling expenses, so that you would not need to have over $750,000 in sundry items.

I Should like to have the minister's opinion of this $2.50 tax on radios. I want to know whether he thinks eleven per cent is a reasonable cost of collecting this tax?
Supply-Transport

Yes, I think eleven per cent is mere than good; it is more than what it would cost to do it in any other way. The hon. member has been critical of this item, but he has not suggested any other way in which it can be done.

I have suggested that a per capita amount be granted to the C.B.C. from the consolidated revenue fund, and in that way it could be collected for a little over one per cent. The minister says this is an economical way to collect this tax, but how would he like to collect all taxes and have it cost eleven per cent? Then those who cannot get reception from the C.B.C. have to pay as well.

I repeat that eleven per cent for collection of this licence fee is not only average; it. is good. I do not know of any other way in which it can be done as economically. My hon. friend has suggested a method, but if it were done in that way it would destroy the independence of the C.B.C.
It would not destroy their independence.

My hon. friend has been doing a lot of talking, and perhaps he will allow me to say something. The hon. member makes a speech on this item every time it comes up. He does not like the $2.50 charge and I do not imagine anybody else does. However, there must be a charge in order to administer this service. At one time it was $2 and then it was increased to $2.50. It has not been changed in the last several years. My hon. friend wants to know what I think of it. I think the fee is a fair one. Perhaps it would be far better if it were possible to do without it, but I think the charge is fair, having regard to the service given. I do not think the average person who sits at home and listens to a program from the C.B.C. or some other station will complain very much about the $2.50. The proof of that lies in the fact that on an average the people pay up fairly well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Five cents a week.

On an average they pay more voluntarily in the radio field than they do in others. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says it is only five cents a week. No one can complain about that. He is entitled to them, but I do not think it would be advisable at this time to do away with the $2.50 fee.

It occurred to me when I first examined this estimate that the cost of collecting the licence fees was unreasonably high, and I have not been entirely convinced that it is not. The minister asserts that they have adopted the best method possible, at least what they believe is the best method possible for the collection of these licence fees. I fancy that the government would be well advised to give further consideration to a less costly method of collection.
It is true that eleven per cent might be quite reasonable, having regard to the methods employed, but I personally feel that the government would be well advised to give further consideration to developing a better method. On page 285 of the estimates appears the following item:
Payments to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in lieu of commissions to issuers.
I should like to have some clarification of that statement. My understanding is that the Department of Transport now remits to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation $2.50 for each $2.50 collected, the cost of collection being a charge against the Department of Transport. I am not positive as to the reason for the change in procedure, unless it was to make the balance sheet of the C.B.C., a public enterprise, look more favourable to the public.
