The authority for the change whereby the Minister of Finance passes directly into consolidated revenue fund the amount of the licence fees is to be found in section 14 (1) (a) of the -Canadian Broadcasting Act, which was amended last year. That amendment reads:
(a) the gross amount of the moneys received in each year from licence fees in respect of private receiving licences and private station broadcasting licences without deducting therefrom any costs of collection or administration.
Prior to that, costs of collection were deducted. That is why this vote has been increased, because it includes not only the cost of administration but the commission to the agents who collect the licence fees.

The minister argued that if so much money was taken from consolidated revenue and handed over to the C.B.C. it would destroy its independence. I want to say something about prosecutions for not having a radio licence. In the first year the prosecutions were practically confined to the city of Toronto. I look upon the radio corporation as one of the most mischievous in this country. They give our hon. friends to our left a great deal of advertising. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I should like briefly to discuss one matter and to ask some questions of the Secretary of State, arising out of the appointment last July by the government of a royal commission to inquire into and report upon the claims of persons of Japanese race arising out of their dispossession of lands and personal property at the time of the movement eastward of those people in the hectic days after the Japanese entry into the war.
I do not intend to go back over the long story which was revealed before the public accounts committee during the session of 1947. I merely make this comment on the facts as elicited by that committee, that, making all allowances

Supply-Secretary of State
for the grave exigencies of the times, the story does not reflect credit upon the administration of the lands and properties of those persons. In most cases those lands were taken from them and sold by the custodian of enemy property, an officer of the government, to another government department at a price which I submit was unwarrantably low and altogether inadequate. That is clearly established by the fact that the price paid by the one government department to the other did not yield more than two-thirds of the assessed valuation; and when some of these properties were valued at a later date it was found that the values established by the officers and committees appointed by the custodian of enemy property were in the aggregate more than twice those established by the other government department, namely the Veterans' Land Act administration, for these properties. In the case of some few which were sold in the open market, the values realized were several times those paid for similar properties by the government department which bought them, namely the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I do not intend to go into that story in greater detail. It was fully covered in the public accounts committee, which submitted a report to this house. In the concluding paragraph of that report, the committee made what I conceive to be an important recommendation. The report of the public accounts committee was tabled in the house on June 17, 1947, and was adopted by the house on motion on June 27. The report will be found set out at pages 536 and 537 of the Journals of the House for 1947. The recommendation in the concluding paragraph of the report reads:
In view of the evidence adduced and in order that more information may be obtained as to the desirability of adjusting any apparent discrimination or loss which may have resulted from the taking over or sale of property of any kind, your committee recommends that a commission be appointed under the provisions of the Inquiries Act to inquire into and report upon the claim of any person of the Japanese race now resident in Canada for alleged loss which resulted from the amount received by him being less than the fair market value of his property at time of sale or loss.
That is the recommendation which was adopted by the house without dissent. I draw attention to the concluding words. The royal commission which was proposed should inquire into and report upon the claim of any person of Japanese race for alleged loss resulting "from the amount received by him being less than the fair market value of his property at time of sale or loss." Some weeks later the government did proceed to appoint a royal commission. That appointment was announced
from Ottawa on July 23, 1947. The government appointed as royal commissioner Mr. Justice Henry I. Bird of the British Columbia Supreme Court. In the statement issued by the Secretary of State announcing the appointment of Mr. Justice Bird as royal commissioner, the terms of the commission of inquiry were set forth. In those terms, the commissioner was instructed to report to the governor in council-and these are the words used:
. . . the claims which, in his opinion, are well founded and the amount which, in his opinion, would fairly and reasonably compensate the claimant for failure of the custodian to exercise reasonable care.
I draw attention to the fact that those terms of reference were very much restricted as compared with those approved by this house on the recommendation of the public accounts committee. They confined the scope of the inquiry to claims arising out of negligence in administration on the part of the custodian of enemy property. That was not a democratic action on the part of the government; and I am sure all hon. members are glad that wiser and more democratic counsels prevailed within the government, because on September 12, 1947, the Minister of Justice announced that the order in council providing for the inquiry into the disposition of the property of persons of the Japanese race had been broadened to meet with suggestions made by the public accounts committee in its report to parliament.
I have looked for that second .order in council of September 12, 1947, enlarging and broadening the terms of reference. I have not been able to find it; but I take it that the press dispatch announcing the passing of the order in council was an accurate statement, and that the commission of inquiry was broadened to conform with the precise terms of the recommendation of the public accounts committee, which was unanimously endorsed by this house. In passing, I would ask the Secretary of State to give the committee the terms of the order in council of September 12 enlarging the scope of the inquiry.
I have seen press dispatches of the same date indicating that the task before the royal commissioner, Mr. Justice Bird, in all probability would consume no less than three years. It is a large task, and no doubt involves a detailed review of many claims, each involving proof of perhaps a number of items, many of them no doubt small, and in circumstances such as to render it perhaps difficult today to obtain complete evidence, by reason of the fact that six j"ears have passed since the date of dispossession.
There are some questions hon. members will wish to ask. I for one wish to ask certain
Supply-Secretary oj State

questions of the Secretary of State with reference to the progress 'being made by the royal commissioner in the heavy task he has assumed. I would ask the Secretary of State if he would be good enough to give a report on the sittings of the commission to date, telling how many claims have been filed, whether the royal commissioner has made any interim report with respect to the claims he has heard, whether any action has been taken by the government on the reports so made, how long the hearings are expected to last, how they are progressing, and other questions of a similar nature.
May I add this in closing, that in acting in conformity with the wishes of the house as expressed on June 27, at the time of the adoption of the report of the committee on public accounts, the government in my opinion has acted properly, although tardily; and it is the hope of many of us that even at this late date justice will be done to those who suffered from a situation which no doubt can be attributed directly to the exigencies of the war, but the impact of which, many of us think, fell unfairly and in a discriminatory manner upon these unfortunate persons of the Japanese race.
I do not wish to open any old wounds. However, at this time I think all hon. members will wish to concentrate on seeing that, so far as possible, at this late date, full efforts are made to redress the property losses which these persons, residents of Canada, sustained in those trying days.

speechtext:
To answer this question, I would say that the commission which was appointed comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice. However I shall secure a copy of the terms of reference as extended by the order in council of September 12, 1947, and see that it is tabled. I understand that in the neighbourhood of 1,800 claims have been filed, that the commissioner has held hearings in Vancouver and throughout the western provinces, that he has completed his hearings in Toronto and is at present completing them in Montreal. I understand that he will be returning to the west and will hold further hearings upon reaching Vancouver.
In the meantime, other judges have been appointed with power to hear evidence, so that the commission may be completed at as early a day as possible. I understand that up to the present no interim report has been filed.

Yes. I thank the hon. member for Eglinton for mentioning this matter and dealing with it in the manner in which he has. I thought of rising myself, but I was not sure whether it would be proper to do so, while the lost property is subject to inquiry by the royal commissioner.
I have a large number of cases which, on the surface, appear to show that a tremendous injustice has been done to many of these people. As a matter of fact, injustice has been done to them, apart from their loss of property. There has been, however, that injustice in the matter of property. I appreciate that it will be difficult to give those claims their proper value, because one has to keep in mind the accretion of property values from the time these people were moved from the Pacific coast to the present.
There can be no point in emphasizing the matter further at this time, but I hope the royal commission will keep in mind not only the value of the property itself and that there will be adequate recompense in that regard, but also the injustice that has been done to these people by uprooting them and scattering them throughout the country in the way it was done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I have in the back of my mind a profound respect for our approach to problems of this kind with regard to the civilization which you, sir, and I, and all of us in Canada enjoy under our present standards. But when my hon. friend rises in his place and uses an expression of the magnitude of "tremendous injustice," when speaking of those people who, while residents of Canada, are not necessarily citizens of this country, I have cause to wonder. These people perhaps feel today, and looking back over the last two or three years hold the view that, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, they have been uprooted, and cast here and there.
This was the uprooting of a few citizens of Japanese origin who were placed in other parts of Canada because we were worried about their proximity to a coastline nearest to their mother country. We thought, in our wisdom, that it was necessary to transplant them-and I use that word for the lack of a better one-or to put them somewhere, so that, geographically, they might not be in a position to act as their hearts might dictate or in a way which might be to the advantage of the race from which they sprang, the land beyond, whence they came.

Supply-Secretary oj State
We have to ask ourselves whether we were not justified in transplanting them at some point removed from the district in which they might be of some assistance to their fellows in their homeland of Japan, thus preventing them from acting in a manner which would be detrimental to those of us who call ourselves Canadians.
I do not think it was a great sacrifice to transfer them from one point to another in this wonderful land of Canada, thus in turn removing them from the temptation of yielding to inclinations which they might have in their minds and hearts, that of being of some assistance to their native land.
I do not think they had to sacrifice much or were greatly embarrassed. I do not think this "tremendous injustice" was quite so tremendous, when I remember what was happening about that time. It was my high privilege in 1944 to be "down under" in Australia when I had the honour of listening for some two hours and a half to General MacArthur's deposition as to what happened when he found himself brushed out or transferred from the Philippines along with a lot of other United States citizens and citizens of other countries. But many were left there to suffer at the hands of the Japanese and the Filipinos in that particular geographical section.
I could not avoid thinking of those who had been left there in that year 1944, because I am one, among other highly privileged citizens, who has passed through his hands in the last two decades close to 1,000 nursing sisters who graduated from the hospital services under a board of which I had the honour to be chairman. General MacArthur got out of the Philippines, but he left behind many of those nursing graduates. They were dear souls, upon many of whom I had had the privilege of pinning that little graduation pin. I could not avoid thinking of those ambitious women who had been left in the Philippines when everyone else had gone.
I think of what happened or what might have happened to those young women who, in the service to humanity, had signed their names to that particular nursing service. Then, in this chamber tonight I had to listen to the hon. member for Vancouver East-I marked his words down-saying that tremendous injustice had been done to the men and women of the Japanese race through being transferred from one part of Canada to another. This has been done under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. How are we to compare this injustice, which is called "tremendous" by the hon. member, with the injustice done by our friends of Japan to these innocent 5849-320
young women of the nursing profession who unfortunately found themselves in Japan and in the Philippines when our friends of the United States boarded steamships and pulled away and left them?
For two and a half hours I interviewed these men who had got away from the Philippines, but during those two and a half hours I thought not of what General MacArthur had to say to those who were privileged to be there-I call the hon. member for Vancouver East as a witness because he sat in the same room-but only of those young women who had been left behind. Yet we hear the hon. member saying that a tremendous injustice has been done to the Japanese through being re-established. I ask him to rise in his place and tell this honourable chamber of those tremendous injustices. He was there in 1944 and he heard the evidence of General MacArthur when we were in Australia. I ask him to state whether or not this Canada of ours has not been abundantly fair to that other part of civilization known as the Japanese race.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

I realize your difficulty, Mr. Chairman, and I realize the difficulty my hon. friend is faced with in trying to bring his mind into position, so that he can deal with a subject which has been greatly enlarged since it was first entered upon.
Mr. KNOWLES1: I rise to a question of privilege. This committee knows that none in
Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

He asked if he could speak, and I informed him that I would be glad to answer any question that he brought up which he had not had an opportunity of bringing up earlier in the evening. However I do not think we should enter into a general discussion on this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I quite realize the minister's position. My only question of privilege is to be permitted to reply to two words which emanated from one section of our organization, namely, "tremendous injustice" to the Japanese race. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, the best thing would be to let those who have occasion to listen or to read draw their own conclusions, and I include you, sir, and every member of this honourable chamber, and more particularly the minister who is piloting these estimates. Tremendous injustices? Just read the record and draw your own conclusions, and I shall be content with the considered judgment of all those who can read.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: A Canadian woman who marries an alien loses her Canadian citizenship. What process has she to go through to get back her Canadian citizenship?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Under the new Citizenship Act a Canadian woman who marries an alien no longer loses her status as a Canadian.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: She does not lose her Canadian citizenship if she marries an alien?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The minister told us the other day that 15,000 citizenship certificates were issued last year. Is that correct? While the minister is looking that up, I notice that we paid close to $200,000 in salaries for the issuance of these 15,000 certificates. That is quite a large sum for 15,000 certificates. Would the minister explain why this great expense is incurred in issuing these certificates? This item deals with the citizenship registra-

tion branch. Further on, there is another item dealing with the citizenship branch. Why are these two items separate?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
They are two entirely separate branches. The registration branch was formerly the naturalization branch. It makes all the investigations that are necessary of those who apply for citizenship. A great deal of work is involved in going through the records of all those who file their applications. The branch has a great deal of correspondence. Last year, for instance, we had 125,000 items of correspondence alone in that department.
Reference has been made to the amount of money expended. This year we are asking for $165,000, of which $10,000 is to microfilm a lot of old records. A great deal of space has been taken up by maintaining files of all those who have been naturalized, and it has been found that a great saving of space can be made by microfilming the important documents and destroying the others.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I take it that the estimate we are now discussing is for citizenship registration?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I notice that there are twenty-one permanent employees. How many temporary employees are there in this branch?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There are eighty-five employees altogether, twenty-one of Whom are permanent.
Mr. COCKERAM1: In other words, the temporary employees are receiving twice the amount in salaries that the permanent employees receive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The temporary employees are receiving $83,000, and the permanent employees, $42,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Just about twice the amount.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. COCKERAM1: In view of the fact that many applicants have now received their papers, why are so many temporary employees needed? Are you going to clean out the temporaries?
'Mr. GIBSON (Hamilton West): It is not a case of having employees who are filling positions which are temporary. The positions will probably be there forever. During the war we did not make employees permanent, because we were reserving the positions for those who came back from overseas. Until the civil service commission has had an opportunity of going

Supply-Secretary oj State
through each department and deciding how many positions should be permanent and how many temporary, we are not able to make permanent appointments of some of those who have been acting as temporary employees. We have at present only twenty^ome permanent employees, but later on I hope that we shall have an establishment providing for a higher number of permanent employees. In that case some of those who have had overseas service will be eligible for permanent appointment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: How many citizenship papers were issued last year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The certificates issued by that branch numbered 25,691.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Surely the minister did not mean that some of these positions would be retained forever. Will the service not gradually grow less and less?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Not if we bring more immigrants into this country. We hope that a great many of them will apply for citizenship.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will the minister withdraw "forever"?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will say indefinitely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Are the temporary employees all appointed through the civil service commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, all of them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What percentage of them are returned men?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: A good many of them are, of course, female clerks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister said a while ago that a Canadian woman who marries an alien does not lose her Canadian citizenship. How long has that been the case? I think there must have been an amendment to the Citizenship Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Since the new Citizenship Act came into operation on January 1, 1947.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have in my riding a Canadian woman who has lived in Canada all her life. She married an alien and was told that she would have to become naturalized herself to regain her Canadian citizenship.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If she married before January 1, 1947, she would have lost her Canadian citizenship and would have to apply again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Could not an amendment be made to the act to make its application retroactive, so that people who are in the position of this woman would not have to go through the whole process of getting citizenship papers?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That proposal has been made. I did not intend to bring in any amendments to the Citizenship Act this session. In Great Britain they are making the provision that those who lost their citizenship through marriage prior to their new citizenship act will be granted British citizenship automatically if they wish to have it. If we bring in an amendment to our Citizenship Act next session consideration will be given to bringing in a similar amendment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: All it needs is a slight amendment to the act. These people are in the position now, and they have to remain that way for another year or so. It is quite important that the amendment should be made. I do not think it would be a serious matter to have it fixed up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I want to say a word on this particular vote. I fail to see why we should have in the estimates two items dealing with registration of citizenship and the citizenship branch. The county court judges have handled this very well since confederation. I fail to see why the government has gone into all this brass-band way of introducing citizenship, and other things. I fail to see any sign of retrenchment in the estimates which the taxpayers back in the constituencies are expecting. Years ago the civil estimates consisted of several million dollars; now they are two billion dollars. How are we to pay for it? The result of this policy was shown in the elections in Ontario the other day. I would far rather see the old system in effect. A great many people do not want to attend these functions where they have orchestras, banquets and all that kind of thing. In my opinion it is unnecessary to become a citizen in that way.
My second point is this. Everybody is desirous of getting away by the end of next week, or by the 25th at the latest. If the government proposes any change in the elections act I think it will be invalid. It is against the constitution to do that without consulting the provinces, especially to substitute proportional voting. On the ballot there will be a list of seven names, and you start crossing them off. I would cross them all off. I would not like to vote for any one of the seven. You start off with first place to one, second place to another, and all that kind of thing.

speechtext:
Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is all I have to say about the minister's estimates. I will tell the government that if they want to close up by the time they have proposed they had better drop some of this legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The hon. member for St. Paul's asked why it was not considered advisable to bring in that amende ment at once. Naturalization laws have been similar throughout the commonwealth, and I think it is desirable to keep them that way so far as possible. A change has not yet been made in Great Britain. I do not know whether it has yet been made in any of the other dominions; I understand not. Consequently we would be well advised to wait and see what they do in Great Britain before we make any change in our existing act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The example I have in mind is that of a woman who married a man before 1947. In the meantime the man became a Canadian citizen. She is still an alien. She was a Canadian before she married.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I want to ask the minister a question with reference to the statement he made a few minutes ago, in which he pointed out that when a Canadian woman marries a foreigner she does not lose her Canadian citizenship. That would mean, I take it, subject to the laws of other countries, that she may be a citizen of Canada and of another country as well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: As a matter of interest, could that be any embarrassment? Are there any cases where double citizenship has been created?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If the woman wants to adopt the citizenship of her husband or his nationality she can, of course, renounce her Canadian citizenship. She has the right to do that if she .wishes. If she wishes to retain her Canadian citizenship she is entitled to do so. There are numerous countries in which there is dual nationality. While it does cause embarrassment on occasions, yet we feel that when a woman gets married she should be permitted to retain her citizenship if she wishes to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If we ever have military conscription for women it would be awkward if they were conscripted for two armies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
We examine these
estimates with the idea of trying to save some money for the taxpayers of this country.
[The Chairman.]
I am wondering why items 429 and 434 could not be combined and a general saving made, because in both of these items there are excessive sums for temporary assistance. They both have printing and stationery, and so on. If our object is to try to cut down expenses there should be some amalgamation of departments of government so that this money could be saved.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That suggestion is prompted only by the fact that the two names are somewhat the same. The work of the two divisions is entirely separate. The citizenship branch is the one in charge of looking after the people who come to this country, assisting them to become good Canadians. For example, we know the communists are hard at work in this country trying to bring pressure to bear on newcomers to Canada. In the- past we have not had any organization to train our people to be good citizens. Education comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces; consequently there is some difficulty in working out programs for the benefit of those new arrivals in Canada. We now have a Canadian citizenship council which is endeavouring to co-ordinate the work of the provinces, of the dominion, and of the welfare organizations throughout this country. The citizenship branch works with the council by keeping in touch with the various ethnic groups in this country. It is having a marked effect, and is able to provide literature to assist newcomers to this country to understand what it means to be a Canadian citizen, and what obligations as well as responsibilities they undertake.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What I have in mind is this. The two departments are handling practically the same thing, so far as I can see. The minister says there is some difference. The minister said that 25,000 naturalization papers were issued last year. The other day he said that 15,000 citizenship certificates had been issued. If these two branches were amalgamated the money saved could be spent on education of newcomers to this country. It seems to me that is where we should spend the money, so that the newcomers may be absorbed into the country as we would like them to be. There is no excuse for having two separate departments dealing with the one subject.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
When the new Citizenship Act was passed, and while it was being discussed in the house, we were informed that all those persons, especially those from the old country who had been in Canada for five or more years prior to the time the act came into force, would be Canadian citizens. I remem-

Supply-Secretary oj State
ber asking the question whether that citizenship would be recognized by the United States. Instances have been brought to my attention where residents of this country for many long years before the Citizenship - Act was passed have had difficulties with United States authorities when they were asked their nationality. When they said they were Canadians the United States authorities asked in what country they were born. Some said England; some said Scotland and some said Ireland. It was drawn to my attention that in one or two instances the United States authorities would not accept the statements made by these persons that they were Canadian citizens, although they had lived here for five, ten, fifteen or twenty years. My question to the minister is this. Will the United States authorities recognize to the fullest extent our new Citizenship Act, without those who are challenged producing papers?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We may say that the United States authorities may recognize that a person going into that country is a Canadian citizen, but for the person entering the country in some cases that unfortunately is not the criterion which is adopted in the United States. The criterion they adopt is where he was born, irrespective of the country to which he happens to belong at the present time, and there is nothing in our law that can make the United States adopt any other attitude.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would that embarrassing situation be obviated were each one to obtain a certificate? Would that certificate be recognized ?	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It would not have any effect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: A foreign-born woman coming to Canada marries a Canadian citizen. After she is here for a year she can make application for citizenship, and three months afterwards she becomes a Canadian citizen?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is a foreign-born woman. Suppose a British subject comes to Canada and marries a Canadian citizen. Does she get citizenship papers sooner?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: They get it in the same way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It takes fifteen months for them anyway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It takes a year and whatever length of time the court takes after that. The minimum is a year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It does not matter whether she is a British subject or foreign born?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
In neither case do they need to file intention to make application?
Mr. GIBSON (Hamilton West); That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: As I recall it, when the Citizenship Act was brought into force, the then secretary of state went around and did a lot of work in the way of instructing newcomers to Canada. I wonder, since he has given up the position, how many temporary employees have been taken on to do the work he did before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The then Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) did that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister said that no change would be made in the act to take care of the situation I mentioned, for the reason that it was desirable to have the law uniform in the commonwealth. Can he give me any particular reason why the situation I have indicated is not different in Canada from that in any other member of the commonwealth? His reasoning does not appeal to me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The act has been in operation for only slightly over a year. It was realized when it was introduced that it would be necessary to make amendments, but I did not consider it advisable to bring in piecemeal amendments until we had an opportunity to find out how it has been working. It is not intended to amend the act this session.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is another point. Some of these people who married aliens in days gone by did not know they would lose their Canadian citizenship and they are faced with that situation. It is a pity that something cannot be done about it. The minister's reasoning with reference to other members of the commonwealth does not appeal to me. I do not see why something could not be done in this direction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
It is usual for members of parliament and, I presume, for other persons to complain when something goes wrong in any department, but when everything goes well and officials deserve credit I believe we are all inclined to overlook the good points about these men and we refrain from saying anything in praise of them.
I wish to take this opportunity, therefore, to mention something favourable. I deal a lot with the Canadian citizenship registration
Supply-Secretary oj State

branch and also with the Canadian citizenship branch, and I may say that the heads of both these branches are doing excellent work for Canada, in the interests of this nation. I would first mention Mr. J. E. Duggan, head of the citizenship registration branch, who is efficient, well-informed and courteous and who is doing a splendid job in his position. His officials and staff are doing likewise.
The head of the citizenship branch, which has to do with education, preparing our newcomers and other persons for citizenship, is Mr. Frank Foulds, about whom I should also like to say a word. In what I say about him I associate his staff. These men and women are really doing a very good job, also in the interests of Canada, and I congratulate the minister and his predecessor, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, on having organized this department on the basis on which it now functions.
The only criticism I have to offer is that the government has not seen fit to put up a building in which these offices would be located. It seems to me that we have reached the time that we must find better quarters for these important branches. These persons are working in cubbyholes, and that is not good enough. I leave that thought with the government, in the hope that they will get busy as soon as possible and erect proper buildings so as to enable these men and women in the two branches I have mentioned to do their work under the best conditions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Last January there was an interesting conference in Montreal at which the Secretary of State was present. It was called by the Canadian citizenship council in collaboration with the Canadian association for adult education, and in that conference participated not only government officials but representatives of voluntary organizations who are interested in the problem of immigrants and prospective new citizens. There were also present representatives of labour organizations and industry. I will not repeat the excellent expressions of opinion we heard there, because the minister himself was present and gave a fine address at a dinner we had, and he is therefore familiar with the situation.
I should like to find out to what extent the recommendations made by the conference have been carried into effect up to this day. I have a copy of the report, as no doubt the minister has, setting out certain recommendations arrived at by the conference, which recommendations were originally suggested by various sections of the conference in panels. In connection with the allocation of responsibility, the committee which had to do with that subject suggested that the conference be called

at the earliest possible day, on the initiative of the federal government and in collaboration with the provincial and municipal authorities, in order to sift over and allocate responsibility for the various services required by new arrivals in this country.
There are certain difficulties to be ironed out, for example hospitalization in some cases, needy widows' allowances, and various other services which ordinarily may fall within the jurisdiction of the province or the municipality. Because immigrants coming to this country are under the jurisdiction of the federal government in the first instance, some of the provinces and municipalities feel that this government should assume some of the initial responsibility, at least, for these services, until these people become fully resident in this country.
Another recommendation passed by this conference, I think unanimously, was in connection with the family allowance. I realize that the actual administration of the family allowance comes under another department; but, since the recommendation was made by this conference, I am sure the minister will have some representations to make-or he may have made them-to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Family Allowances Act provides, for example, that a person must live in this country for three years before becoming eligible. This conference pointed out that a certain amount of hardship results from this requirement. This is the argument of the committee which dealt with that matter, if I may put it on the record:
Family allowances are not paid to newcomers in Canada until they have resided in the country for three years. The new arrival is operating with additional handicaps at best. It seemed to the group unfortunate that the children of newcomers should suffer the further handicap of being denied the benefits family allowances could give them, particularly in view of the fact that normally their parents would be earning their lowest income at the beginning of their residence in Canada. The greatest need for family allowances is precisely during the period after arrival. It was distinctly unfortunate that these children should receive this additional handicap for three years.
Later on, a recommendation was made in definite words, to this effect:
That the Department of Health and Welfare be asked to modify the three-year resident provisions of the Family Allowances Act and its regulations so that the children of new arrivals to Canada will receive the benefits before three years.
A couple of weeks ago I happened to be in the Okanagan valley, where I met a gentleman who had just arrived from South Africa.

Supply-Secretary oj State
He had brought with him his wife and six children, and told me it cost him more than $3,000 to make the trip. He was greatly disappointed to find that, in spite of being a British subject and in spite of having given up certain services in his own country, his family were not eligible for the family allowance in this country, and he felt something should be done about the matter. That may be just one case, but probably it could be multiplied by many thousands.
I am not going to pursue this point further, because I realize that the administration of that act comes under another department. But this conference, which was quite representative, passed a recommendation asking this department to request the Department of National Health and Welfare to make a change at some time in the near future, and I hope the minister will take that into consideration.
I want now to say just a word about some of the other work done at this conference, which I thought was of great importance and of a very high character. Recommendations were made in connection with naturalization and the pre-naturalization education that should be given newcomers to this country. I hope the department is taking full advantage of the views expressed at this conference and the excellent recommendations made; because, as one who, in the past, has taken some part in the education of new immigrants to this country, I can say to the minister that many of the handicaps I experienced at that time would be overcome if the recommendations of this conference were accepted by the citizenship branch, and adequate financial provision were made to carry through a program of education.
I also want to add a word to what was said by the hon. member who preceded me, with respect to the citizenship council and the citizenship branch. I have in my hand a number of pamphlets published by various agencies, all of which are available either from the Canadian citizenship council, which has its headquarters here in Ottawa at 166 Marlborough avenue-and I am putting that on record in case someone wants to look it up later-or at the citizenship branch of the Department of the Secretary of State. For example, I have in my hand one entitled, "Everyman's Guide to Canada's Parliament." It is not a very large publication, but I recommend it to all hon. members, so that we may see ourselves as others see us. It will enable them to get a bird's-eye view of how we are seen in this house. Another one is entitled, "How to become a Canadian citizen," and is published by the Canadian citizenship
branch. It is also an excellent booklet which should be widely distributed and which people should be encouraged to read. I have here another one called, "Our Canadian Government," which is also available through the Canadian citizenship council or the Canadian citizenship branch; and a fourth one entitled "'Citizenship; the Teacher's Problem."
Just here I should like to say that in many of the rural areas of Canada much of the work of providing the elementary or primary education for new arrivals will fall upon the shoulders of rural teachers,. who will have to do that work after their regular duties are finished. That is so, because in those areas they have not the facilities which are provided in larger centres through either voluntary organizations or government branches. So I would urge the minister, in co-operation with the various provincial departments of education, to provide every possible facility and encouragement, in the way of both finances and available material, for these schoolteachers, who do a valuable job in the evenings after their day's work is through, and who are contributing a great deal to the future citizens of our country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There has been a good deal of discussion concerning the employees of this department. Before asking the question I have in mind, I should like to direct the minister's attention to the fact that the estimates for his department amount to a total of $1,437,521, of which almost 50 per cent-to be exact I think it is 43 per cent-or 8591,297 is required for temporary assistance. I should like to know from the minister how many of those temporary employees are engaged by the year and how many are just here today and gone tomorrow. I should like to know also how many temporary employees are drawing this amount of money, which accounts for some 43 per cent of the total vote for his department,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext:
In the 1947 session the patent office received more attention than it had received in many previous sessions, and I suggest it was well that it did. This interest arose in the first instance in connection with a bill the government introduced, proposing certain extensive amendments to the Patent Act. The bill was referred to the committee on banking and commerce; and that committee, seized of the importance of studying the conditions in the patent office, recommended to the house that it should be empowered to inquire into the administration of the patent office in regal'd/ to staff, office space, equipment and the like, and to report to the house in relation thereto. That report was submitted to the house on March 4, 1947, and was adopted the same day.
An extensive study of conditions in the patent office was carried out by the committee on banking and commerce. The facilities available to the patent commissioner and his staff were studied at first hand by a subcommittee of the committee on banking and commerce, with the result that an extensive report covering the studies of the banking and commerce committee and its subcommittee was tabled in the house on July 15, 1947. No motion was made for the adoption of the report. The committee will recall that that was only two days before prorogation. Although not adopted by the house, the report nevertheless has behind it the full authority of the committee on banking and commerce, following an intensive study.
The first fact that should be remembered in any approach to the question of the adequacy or inadequacy of the staff and facilities of the patent office is this, that the patent office is a money-maker for the government. It should not be thought that this office is a bill of expense to the taxpayer. While the committee is called upon to vote certain appropriations for the patent office, nevertheless over a long period of years the fees earned through that office have considerably exceeded government expenditures in respect thereto.
In the banking and commerce committee a year ago the figures for the ten years from 1936 to 1946 were tabled. Those figures are to be found at page 13 of the proceedings of the committee for 1947. I shall not trouble the committee by going into the figures in detail, but I shall place on record the aggregate results of those ten years of operation.
The expenditures in connection with the administration of the patent office in that ten-year period aggregated $2,048,000 in round

Supply-Secretary oj State
figures, whereas the fees earned through the patent office aggregated $3,525,000. Thus in the ten-year period I have mentioned the patent office earned for the government a net revenue of $1,500,000. The sum of $3,525,000 received in the ten-year period, together with the additional sums paid in fees in the two and a half years since, were paid by persons doing business with that office, who, in return for the payment of fees, are entitled to expect prompt and efficient service.
I wish to make it as clear as I possibly can, here and now, that I believe the commissioner of patents and his staff are rendering as efficient service as it is possible for them to render under present conditions. I believe the commissioner of patents has rendered great service, and is an able official; and I am sorry that on him has fallen the brunt of the problem of functioning or trying to make his office function under great difficulties and handicaps. These are handicaps, not only of inadequate space, but also of inadequate staff. One of the reasons the staff is inadequate is that the space is inadequate, and there has not been space enough to accommodate a staff adequate to meet the needs of the office.
The committee's report is found in the Journals of the Home for the 1947 session, at pages 910 to 915, and that report demonstrates the situation clearly. It sets out a condition which, in my opinion, cannot be permitted to continue. In brief, at that time the patent office was three years in arrears with its work. The backlog of applications uncompleted was over 31,000, which represents between two and a half and three years work of the patent Office. At that time the office could not keep abreast of current work. The situation in regard to staff was serious, because salaries paid at the prevailing scale were inadequate to attract personnel having the necessary technical qualifications. The office of the commissioner of patents had suffered a serious and substantial loss of personnel during the war, particularly technical personnel. I need not tell the committee that personnel of that kind is difficult to obtain in times like these. When private industry is offering substantially greater rewards to personnel possessed of the qualifications of which a patent examiner must be possessed, it is obvious that the patent office cannot, under present circumstances, expect to retain its personnel, let alone recruit additional necessary staff, unless it is prepared to offer adequate remuneration for the purpose.
After a study of the situation, it was the view of the banking and commerce committee that the salary scale obtaining at the patent office was quite inadequate to attract the additional personnel required. Some headway has been made, because the commissioner was able to report to the banking and commerce committee a year ago that he had recently been able to recruit some additional personnel, both technical and non-technical, but the situation with respect to adequacy of staff as described to the banking and commerce committee still exists.
The problem of inadequacy of staff was closely related to the problem of inadequate accommodation. The fact of the matter is that, even if the commissioner had been able to enlist the additional technical personnel needed at that time, he would not have had any place in which to put them. It was an extraordinary situation. These trained examiners were working two or three to an office, sometimes quite a small office, under conditions which greatly impeded the efficiency of their operations. Valuable records were stored under conditions which made it very difficult to have access to them. There was a crying need for additional accommodation.
I hope I am a reasonable person. I do not expect the government to create buildings out of thin air. I do not expect them to be able to bring into existence overnight, building accommodation when there is a considerable scarcity of it in Ottawa. Nevertheless the situation that existed a year ago was most serious. The public dealing with the patent office was not receiving the service they should have received. I submit that this problem is entitled to a position of leading priority among the government projects for the post-war period.
Again I emphasize that the office of the commissioner of patents is a money-maker. Canadians and others making application to the patent office are entitled to receive service commensurate with the fees they are paying. It is quite unfair that the government should continue to derive a substantial net profit from the operations of this office and not give the service to which those paying the fees are entitled.
The situation was advanced a stage further by the legislation which parliament enacted at the 1947 session. I think the Secretary of State will be the first to admit that the banking and commerce committee did a most useful service last year in connection with the revision of the Patent Act. The amendments which were introduced in the house and referred to the committee were carefully reviewed. Many changes were made and further amendments in the Patent Act were introduced. I think it is generally conceded that
5058
Supply-Secretary of State

the result was a much more workable Patent Act than was the case before the 1947 legislation came into effect.
But there is one curious result. The increase in fees was enacted by parliament on the assumption that the patent office would be equipped to give improved service. Section 19 of the bill which was adopted last year introduced into the act a new section 17 which had the effect of increasing practically the entire scale of fees. The note to that section of the bill read as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to secure revenue from which to defray expenses involved in the printing of specifications and drawings of patents, as provided for in section 26 of the principal act.
It is a matter of record that at that time there were not in the patent office facilities for the printing of specifications and patents. When compared with the patent office in Washington and patent offices in other countries, that was a serious shortcoming. The committee concerned itself at some length with the printing of specifications and drawings, and in its report to the house it made recommendations with respect thereto.
I think at this stage I might read the three recommendations with which the committee concluded its report, and which are to be found on pages 913 and 914 of the Journals of 1947.
They read as follows:
Staff: Attached to this report is an appendix showing the minimum staff which should be supplied to the patent office, and your sub-committee recommends that this staff should he supplied at the earliest possible date.
The appendix proposed a substantial increase in the number of employees in the patent office. The next recommendation reads:
Office space:	Attached to this report is an
appendix showing the amount of office space, storage space, et cetera, required by the patent office, and your sub-committee recommends that when the government is expanding its building program for the housing of government departments, suitable space both as to size and of fireproof construction, should be made available to the patent office.
I observe here that the reference to the subcommittee is to the subcommittee of the banking and commerce committee. Its report was adopted by the banking and commerce committee. The appendix shows that not less than 109,590 square feet of floor space is required. The third recommendation reads:
Printing of patents:	Your sub-committee
recommends that a printing plant by the offset process should be installed in the patent office for the printing of patents, specifications, claims

and drawings, and that the necessary staff be employed to operate the same at the earliest possible date.
May I say that the committee considered the cost of printing specifications and drawings. It had before it a report from the king's printer, indicating that the cost would be substantial. It also had a report indicating that if the offset process were used the cost of printing could be materially reduced; in fact it would be only a fraction of what it would cost if it were done in the office of the king's printer. That was the reason why the recommendation was made that facilities be provided in the patent office for the printing of specifications and drawings by the offset process.
We had, therefore, a situation where parliament was passing a measure to increase the fees to be charged in the patent office for the purpose, as stated in the note to the bill, of securing revenue to defray the expenses involved in the printing of specifications and drawings of patents. I ask the Secretary of State to give the committee a report on the progress that has been made toward providing facilities in the patent office for the printing of specifications and drawings. I am informed that no printing has been done, that increased fees are being charged but that the service for which the increased fees were imposed is not being given.
I ask the minister also to give a full report on the progress, if any, that has been made toward implementing all the recommendations of the committee. I recognize, Mr. Chairman, that these recommendations -have not behind them the full weight that would have been attached to them had they been adopted in the house by formal resolution; but I am bold enough to venture this statement, that if the report of that committee had been discussed in the house it would have met iwith the endorsement of the house. I remind hon. members that that report was brought in, unfortunately, only two days before prorogation in July last year. The report had behind it the full weight of the unanimous support of the banking and commerce committee, after a lengthy and intensive investigation.
Some arrangements are, I am told, being made to move some parts of the patent office into the Canadian building. In a matter as serious as this I do urge upon the minister that the committee is entitled to receive from him a very full report. It is not a situation that can reflect credit upon the administration of governmental affairs in this country that the patent office should be permitted to continue for from two and a half to three years in

Supply-Secretary of State
arrears with its work. That is not, I emphasize again, the fault of the commissioner or of the staff. Sometimes one wonders that they do as well as they have done, labouring under their present handicaps. I submit that this is a matter which must receive immediate attention. The situation is so serious that it must receive top-ranking priority among the projects which the government ought to undertake immediately.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad that my hon. friend spoke as well as lie did on this subject, because I am sure that too many members of the house are ignorant of the situation in the patent office. The patent office in this country has always been the poor child of the government; it has always been treated as though it were something that was not needed, although, as the hon. member pointed out, it has been a revenue-producing branch ever since its inception. It is high time that more members of the house took an interest in the patent office.
In the United States the patent office is not a revenue-producing branch. It is run as a service to encourage inventors to invent and produce for the benefit of the public. But in this country we have never encouraged inventors by the service we have given them in the patent office.
The staff of the patent office is very good. We have a very good commissioner, very good examiners, and a devoted clerical staff. But we have too few of them, and the staff is underpaid. I had hoped, after last year's report by the banking and commerce committee, that there would have been a substantial revision upward in the salaries of the technical men in the patent office and also a revision upward of the salaries of the clerical staff. Mind you, it is not ordinary work that some of the clerical staff do in the patent office, but there are more grade 1 and grade 2 clerks who have been around there for twenty years as grade 1 or grade 2 than there are in any other department of the government. They have been overlooked altogether. That is not the fault of the commissioner of patents. It is rather the fault of the heads of the department. I believe that the cabinet ministers who have been in charge of it from time to time have thought that, since it was a good revenue-producing branch, it should be left as such. I suggest that we take a little more serious view. The staff is too small. I have been dealing with patents since I was eighteen years of age, and it has always been the same old story in the patent office. Everything is always a couple of years behind, and the
result is that as patent solicitors we get complaints from our clients who think that we have taken their money and are not doing anything to help them, that we are robbing them, because they do not hear from us for eight or nine months.
The staff of the patent office do their best. If a case is exceptional we will get a special order; but we cannot ask that all our cases be considered as special cases, and therefore the impression is given to the United States public, who are the greatest contributors to the patent office, and to our Canadian clients, that we are delinquent in our duty. That is not a good situation for solicitors and lawyers to be in. I therefore ask that the staff of the patent office be increased, but you cannot increase the staff if you do not pay reasonable salaries to the technical personnel which forms the patent office. Further, I ask that the clerical staff be enlarged and that, whatever the civil service commission may say, there be a proper classification of the clerical staff and that they be paid salaries which are reasonable for clerks or technical men.
I understand that some space has been found in the Canadian building, but part of the patent office is still in the Langevin block. The most important part of the patent office is the search room and the library. We should have a proper search room and a proper library immediately, because that is the very life of the patent office. That is where the public must search to find out whether an invention is new. The records are in the library and in the search room. At present all that is in one room, in cramped quarters, with no facilities for solicitors to sit down and study. As a result, the government is losing revenue. It follows, of course, that when we have printed records of all the patents already issued, searches can be made much more easily, but I understand that we cannot have printed patents within one year. Indeed, I am sure that it will take another year or two before a start is made on the printing of patents.
I spoke to the commissioner some time ago, and I understand that the printing bureau is now in a position to print patents at a cost which would compare with that suggested by the banking and commerce committee. It is true that the recommendation made last year by the banking and commerce committee was made with a view to offsetting the cost of printing patents; but I must say that the increase was not very substantial, and it does not compare at all with the fees which are being charged in other countries. As a matter of fact I consider that the fees are still too
5060
Supply-Secretary of State

low and it is working a hardship on this country, because two-thirds of the fees which come into the patent office come from the United States.
There is another small matter which I think should be rectified. When we file an application for a patent in the United States of America we have to take our affidavits to the United States consul here. The Secretary of State should make representations to the patent office in Washington, so that it should not be necessary for Canadians to take an affidavit before a notary public in this country to have it authenticated by the United States consul. We have never asked for that from United States citizens. I do not think Canadians should be put to that extra cost when filing an application for a patent in the United States.
I hope that the Secretary of State, who I know has progressive ideas on this matter, will see to it that sufficient space is secured in the Canadian building, if that is to be the building to house the patent office. By "sufficient" I mean ample. I hope he will remember my remarks about the search room and the library. If we had more facilities to search and study patents we would have more revenue. More people would come here to find out about our patents; they would secure copies of patents, and they would file applications. If we had more service to give we would find that a great number of United States patents which are not filed in this country would be filed, because people would expect that they could exploit their patents within a reasonable time. At the present time, many inventors are discouraged because they know they cannot get a patent for perhaps two or three years, and in that time the patent would be of no use to them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have sat here year after year listening to criticism being levelled at the patent office and the commissioner of patents. He has been criticized; the division has been criticized severely for long delays in the issuance of patents, and that sort of thing. I wish to say right now that, while I am not an authority-I am not a patent attorney-there are more delays created in the offices of the legal profession and in the offices of patent attorneys in Canada than there are in the office of the commissioner of patents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: On a point of privilege, I hope the Iron, member does not refer to me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a direct question in connection with the matter of accommodation for the patent office? As I

understand the present situation, the patent office is in two buildings; part of it is in the Langevin block and part of it in the Canadian building. The situation is almost as intolerable from the standpoint of getting business done as it was before. There is something behind the scenes somewhere which is stopping the patent office from getting into the Canadian building. We had better bring that out in the open. I understand that there is another department of government there that will not get out. If that is so, we ought to know about it. There ought to be some liaison, or some pressure brought to bear on the department and the cabinet to see that that department does get out, because we cannot allow this intolerable situation to continue, as I see it, with one part of the department in one building and the other part in another. The minister had better bring this thing out in the open and tell us exactly what the situation is, and who is preventing the patent office from getting into its proper quarters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel speaks as if there were some secret or hidden mystery about this patent office. There is nothing that I am ashamed to mention.
I want to answer what the hon. member for Eglinton had to say in regard to the work of the office. As bon. members know, at one time, before the new plans were made, the patent office was spread around in about six different buildings in Ottawa. I am glad to say that we were able to get accommodation in the Canadian building. The first step that we took was to bring in all the outlying branches of the patent office from the various buildings into the Canadian building. We were not able to get the whole Canadian building at once. We have now got a good part of it, but two floors in the Canadian building are occupied by the wartime prices and trade board, and one floor by the succession duties branch of the Department of National Revenue. These have not yet been vacated. It is expected that we shall have the whole building, the part that has been allotted to us, within the next few months.
The printing of patents was authorized. A question arose as to whether the patent office itself should undertake that work. After some careful consideration of the matter, we worked out an agreement between the patent office and the printing bureau, under which the printing bureau will do the work at the patent office. That is, the printing bureau, which has experienced men, and has knowledge of the machinery required, is purchasing the necessary equipment which will be installed in the

Supply-Secretary oj State
Canadian building in the patent office; but the actual printing work will be done by contract with the printing bureau on the premises of the patent office.
There has been some increase in staff; but, as the hon. member for Eglinton said, it is not easy to get the qualified men, and we still have some vacancies for examiners, which is, of course, a technical position. It is not easy to fill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister has not yet told us what is the hold-up in the Canadian building. I am anxious to know what the obstacle is and who is there that we cannot get out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend was talking to somebody else when I mentioned it. I said that at the present time the wartime prices and trade board are still in the building. It is expected that they shall be out very shortly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I understood that this was to be done months ago. Why is the wartime prices and trade board there? Has that board any special priority in the building when the patent office is much more important than the board?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think the national defence library has altogether pulled out. Although they were occupying space on the ground floor, they have started to move. I do not think they have all their books out of that part. Of course, when the other departments moved out of the other parts of the building a certain amount of redecorating and rearrangement of the rooms on the upper floors was necessary, which took some time, to make them suitable for the patent office.
