speechtext:
When will the entire
patent office be moved to the Canadian building?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The last report I have received is that the whole move will be completed within the next few months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
In a few months. I am asking these questions with a definite objective in view. I am really concerned about the position of the patent office. From the information I get from many quarters I think it is a scandal to allow this office to be hung up in this way. The minister ought to go to the Minister of Finance or whoever is responsible and clear this thing up and get the wartime prices and trade board out. 'Let us cut all
the red tape that this thing seems to be tied up with. You will never get in there if you do not do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I want to put in a word here. We have had two powerful statements tonight from persons who are familiar with this situation. We have had the hon. member for Eglinton recalling to the committee what was done a year ago when the banking and commerce committee reported to the house. That happened almost a year ago. Then we had the hon. member for Ottawa East giving in great detail some of the defects. The minister has given an answer recognizing that there is a situation to deal with. I got no sense from the minister that this was regarded as something which had absolutely top priority and which should be done. I should like to ask the minister this question. As I understand it, it has been said that the work is some two and a half to three years behind. The seriousness of that in several ways has been made clear. It is not merely the inconvenience to those who are putting in applications, not merely the discouragement to inventors who might put in applications, but actually the great loss in business probably to the office because the facilities are not available. Is there some plan by which this will be dealt with? Is there a plan under which these arrears are to be grappled with, so that they will be wiped out within a given time?
The minister says, and indeed it had already been indicated by those who spoke before him, that it is difficult to get men. That is clear. But are steps being taken to meet this difficulty? Are special inducements being offered? Surely this is something that is in a different category'. We have boards and institutions of all kinds, about the value of which we may have great differences of opinion, but here is something on which everyone is agreed. It is generally agreed that the public wishes to have this branch put in the highest state of efficiency. I would ask the minister whether there is now a plan whereby these arrears will be brought down. Is there any plan whereby staff will be got and the necessary steps taken to get them, so that within a reasonable time these arrears will have been wiped off? Nothing short of that is a satisfactory answer to the arraignment, and it is an arraignment to which the committee has listened tonight.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not an authority on the patent law, or he would realize that, when reference is made to the fact that patents are in arrears,

Supply-Secretary oj State
that is a standard condition. The length of time they are in arrears is another matter. When applied for, a patent is not issued within a week or within a month. I think the Canadian record at the present time compares quite favourably with the record of other countries in the average length of time it takes to issue a patent. It does not depend entirely on the activity of the patent office. They receive an application and they write back and make certain requisitions, and that goes back to the solicitor who is handling the application. He then calls in the inventor, and perhaps a period of six months goes by before a reply comes into the patent office. That -is dealt with; there has to be a second application. It goes back to the solicitor, and in some cases it is a matter of six years before the patent is obtained, depending on the speed with which applicants apply for patents. Sometimes they do not wish to have a patent issued too early. Having filed their application, they are protected, but they may not want it at once. They may not want time to run against them, and sometimes there is a purposeful delay in answering the questions of the department. Sometimes six months go by without a letter being answered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister will admit that the evidence given last year before the committee was that when the application was filed in the first place it would be acknowledged by the department; but that a matter of eight months would go by before any further step would be taken by the department. Has the situation changed in that regard in the last year? The department was not itself in a position to have the necessary work done by the examiners for a period of eight months. Has that situation changed?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes. The situation has improved. We are not in a fully satisfactory position and shall not be until we get into one building, and we want an increased staff. I would not say the work of the patent office is unsatisfactory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is the minister not seized of the fact, which came out before the committee last year, that one basic necessity in the proper working of the patent office is adequate housing for the whole staff in one building?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I agree.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will the minister tell us tonight that within a matter of a few months he will have the office together in one building?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is right,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister is perfectly right when he says that I am not an expert, but I have listened to two hon. gentlemen who I thought and still think are experts, and when I heard the word "arrears" used I took it in its ordinary sense. The minister says, in effect, that things are not so bad, that there is no real urgency. If that is the spirit of the approach to this question, that there is no real sense of urgency, then I suggest that other persons who are more competent than I am should say whether there is, in fact, such urgency.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I am bound to say to the minister that his answer concerning delays in the patent office does not strengthen the position he has taken on this matter. The minister will be the first to recognize that we who have spoken on the question are trying to strengthen his hands in an effort to see that the patent office situation is cleared up. We are trying to help him to obtain accommodation and personnel, and his answer that the situation is satisfactory is entirely inadequate. It is a most incomplete answer to say that there are inevitable delays in dealing with patent matters. Of course there are. It takes time to make due examination of patents. There must be correspondence; there must- be citations, and all that sort of thing. No one expects the patent office to function on applications the day they are received; nevertheless.it is quite inadmissible for the minister to say that the patent office is not working unsatisfactorily at the present time. The commissioner before the committee said, not once but many times, that the public is not receiving from the patent office the service to which it is entitled. Is the minister going to say, after that, that the office is working satisfactorily? I hold that, through no fault of the commissioner and the staff, the office is not working satisfactorily. It is working in a manner far from satisfactory. When we have the irrefutable evidence, taken before the banking and commerce committee last year, that the time lag in dealing with these patents runs from two and a half to three years from the date of receipt, no one may say that the office 'is working satisfactorily.
On the question of accommodation in the Canadian building, may one express the hope that the minister will be firm and insistent in pressing for due accommodation for the needs of the patent office. I had. hoped that we would receive something more favourable from the minister than the statement that in a matter of months the patent office will have completed its move into the Canadian building. What we should have and are entitled to is a carefully prepared, comprehensive, reasoned and complete statement giving us the best estimate he can give us at the present time, first of all, as to what results have been achieved since last autumn and secondly, as to our expectations based on the best analysis he can make of our foreign trade position and the best analysis he can make of what we may expect in the development of our trade. It is clear from these figures that the imposition of controls has resulted in a diminution of imports and that the greatest saving to date has been in the case of automotive vehicle tariff items 438a and 439b, which were made effective on November 18, 1947. It should further be borne in mind that imports have been admitted in many cases in schedule III where contracts were made prior to November 18, 1947. It is clear that these cases will become of less importance as time goes on although it was recognized in advance that there would be a large number of them at the beginning of the program.
Methods of administration have been devised which take account of the various problems which arise in the import of schedule III items. Wherever possible, import quotas have been applied, or dollar allotments as they are called. In most cases these have followed the general pattern of the formula applied to imports of the automobile industry which I explained in this house at an earlier date. These dollar allotments have been found most suitable in controlling the imports of parts for production use enumerated in schedule III.
In other cases not subject to these dollar allotments, applications are received for import permits on an individual basis. Until the end of May a total of $21-5 million of import authorizations have been granted in this way, $14 million for imports from the United States and S7-5 million for imports from other countries. This has involved thousands of individual applications, each of which had to be carefully screened.
A third system has been evolved to deal with anyone engaged in a project such as the construction of an industrial plant. Applications may be made for blanket approval of all the imports necessary for the particular project. Project approvals which are issued in these circumstances are, in effect, an assurance that individual shipment permits will be issued as they are needed. Up to the end of May, a total of 232 project applications had been approved. A large proportion of these cover the expansion of industries which will either increase exports or diminish our dependence on imports on a sound economic basis. About forty project applications have been approved for the replacement of obsolete and uneconomical equipment. A number of these latter were in the textile industry. Seventeen of these project permits deal with public service projects, of which by far the most important is the hydro-electric power development now taking place throughout Ontario.
The total value of materials still required for these 232 projects amounts to some $495
million, $73 million of which is material covered by schedule III to be imported from the United States during 1948 and subsequent years. Almost every Canadian industry of any size has been affected by this project authorization system. Apart from public utilities in Ontario, the industries which account for the largest expenditures in the above total are pulp and paper, textiles, petroleum, chemicals and processed foods and beverages.
Schedule III was not designed to place drastic limitations on industry. Quite the reverse; it was intended to promote industrial growth in the most constructive possible way. This program is being developed every day. Imports of capital goods were in danger of going beyond what we could afford to spend in United States dollars, but drastic curtailment would have been undesirable. It would have impeded industry's plans and would have caused unemployment and attendant difficulties in many parts of the country. Hasty or ill-considered action might well have altered our course from our present booming prosperity to the reverse, recession and falling incomes. This has been avoided. New industries are being established in Canada all the time to continue the development and further integration of our national economy. Thus the program is not merely to save dollars in the short run, but also to assist industry as a whole to spend our scarce United States dollars where they will do the most good for our future development. The co-operation on the part of industry has been excellent throughout, and there has been evidence of widespread public desire to assist in solving the dollar exchange problem.
Imports of steel provide a good illustration of efforts made to obtain adequate supplies of an important basic material for Canadian industry. We are not anxious to cut down our steel; on the contrary we are anxious to import as much as we can get, consistent with the allocation of steel which must be made in the United States to many other important uses. In the first quarter of 1948, tonnage of structural steel imports subject to control was about fifty-seven per cent higher than in the first quarter of 1947, although about sixteen per cent below the fourth quarter of 1947.

effect a total saving, on this tariff item alone, of about 355,000,000 in 1948. Additional savings on automotive parts were estimated to bring the total saving on automobile imports up to $70,000,000 or $75,000,000 in 1948. It looks now as if savings of this magnitude will be attained. Nearly all the reduction in imports thus far is attributable to diminished imports of complete vehicles from the United States. The import formula for the automobile industry has permitted the continued imports of parts at a high level. Along with this, production in the Canadian automobile industry bids fair to be comparable with the high levels of last year. In the first quarter of 1948, roughly 60,000 vehicles were produced. Types of vehicles will be manufactured in Canada which were previously imported from the United States, and at least one manufacturer has been hastening plans for the Canadian production of his car which was previously imported. Another manufacturer is moving into the production of motor coaches in Canada. A number of Canadian industries have expanded the manufacture of automobile parts and sub-assemblies which were previously imported. They include new types of wheels, non-vacuum fuel pumps, hub, drum and transmission assemblies and others.
The industrial expansion which we are encouraging can best be illustrated by referring to a few of the industries for which imports of machinery and equipment have been authorized.
Among our largest imports last year were textile fabrics, that is, cottons, rayons and woollens. These amounted to about S180 million and were largely imported from the United States. Well over one-half of the imports consisted of cotton fabrics. As hon. members know, it has been necessary to make large reductions in our imports of cottons and rayons from the United States and, especially in the case of cotton fabrics, import restrictions will sharply reduce the supply available for the domestic market. At present there are a number of large expansion and modernization projects under way in all branches of the textile industry that will contribute substantially to a reduction of our imports of these materials as well as of yarns and fibres, and will increase efficiency in the industry. These projects will not only aid in our immediate dollar saving program and alleviate material shortages but also contribute to the improvement of our long-term dollar position. In these respects the expansion of our cotton industry will be most important. I can add, too, that the completion of a rayon plant now under way will make it less necessary to import rayon fibres and yarns.

In the pulp and paper industry there is a large expansion program under way to increase our production of a number of products, particularly for export to the United States. Some of these projects will process pulp previously exported; others will convert our paper into containers and other paper products now being imported. In the past, Canada has imported a substantial amount of copper and brass products. In this industry, too, a large expansion project now under way should materially reduce our dependence on imports. The same is true of our asbestos industry. Heretofore, a large proportion of our asbestos has been exported as a raw material, and it has been necessary for us to import various manufactured asbestos products. A number of large projects now under way will not only increase our production of asbestos but, in particular, increase our production of manufactured products for both the domestic and export markets.
I have already referred to recent developments in our automobile industry, and there are similar developments in a number of our other secondary manufacturing industries. For example, one of the largest United States manufacturers of automatic washing machines is to establish a plant in Canada for the manufacture of his products. The Canadian plant will supply most of the export markets already established by the United States parent company, and at the same time will manufacture repair parts for the world market, including the United States.
